message.content:
You are doing part of a literature novelty check for a planned preregistered study. Return findings as your final message (no report files).

PLANNED STUDY (context): Using the Open Anchoring Quest (OpAQ) dataset (Röseler, Weber, Helgerth, Stich et al. 2022, J Open Psychol Data, doi 10.5334/jopd.67; OSF ygnvb; 412 anchoring items, 96 studies, 88,914 estimates), test how the PROPORTIONAL anchoring index (AI = (central estimate under high anchor − under low anchor)/(high anchor − low anchor)) changes with anchor extremity, at the item level, against simulated predictions of four process models. The OpAQ meta-analysis (Röseler & Schütz, "Hanging the anchor off a new ship", PsyArXiv 10.31234/osf.io/wf2tn) regressed Hedges' g on mean relative anchor distance.

TASK: For every work that cites OpAQ (10.5334/jopd.67) or the meta-analysis preprint (10.31234/osf.io/wf2tn), determine whether it REUSED OpAQ data (vs merely citing) and summarise what it did (design, measure, key numbers), with emphasis on anything touching anchor distance/extremity, proportional adjustment, or computational models. Known citers (OpenAlex):
- Röseler et al. 2024, "Correction: The Open Anchoring Quest Dataset", JOPD, 10.5334/jopd.92 — what was corrected (item/trial counts? variables?).
- Röseler, Weber, Helgerth, Stich et al. 2024, "Measurements of Susceptibility to Anchoring are Unreliable", Meta-Psychology, 10.15626/mp.2022.3236.
- Röseler, Incerti, Rebholz, Seida et al. 2023, "Falsifying the Insufficient Adjustment Model: No Evidence for Unidirectional Adjustment From Anchors", PsyArXiv 10.31234/osf.io/jztk2 — check for a published version (journal) and what it found (numbers).
- Mayer & Heck 2025 PBR 10.3758/s13423-024-02619-9 "Modeling dependent group judgments: sequential collaboration" (computational model; does it use OpAQ?).
- Fischer, Mayer, Kimmerle 2026 JBDM 10.1002/bdm.70063.
- Onuki & Ueda 2025 Commun Psychol 10.1038/s44271-025-00276-9 "Range nudges".
- Barrera-Lemarchand et al. 2024 Psych Sci 10.1177/09567976241252138.
- Reimer et al. 2024 Sustainability 10.3390/su16062540 "Thermostat anchors".
- Navarre, Didierjean, Hazif Thomas 2024 L'Année psychologique 10.3917/anpsy1.244.0591 (review of 50 years of anchoring — does it discuss extremity/AI?).
- Young, Speekenbrink et al. 2026 Cogn Psychol 10.1016/j.cogpsych.2026.101796 (another agent reads this in depth; just note whether it uses OpAQ).
- Stöcker 2024 thesis 10.20378/irb-96573; Shiddieqi et al. 2024 Scientax (just classify briefly).
ALSO extend coverage beyond OpenAlex: query Semantic Scholar (no key): https://api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1/paper/DOI:10.5334/jopd.67/citations?fields=title,year,externalIds,venue,authors&limit=100 and the same for DOI:10.31234/osf.io/wf2tn; also WebSearch (load via ToolSearch "select:WebSearch,WebFetch") for "Open Anchoring Quest", "OpAQ anchoring", "Open Anchoring Quest dataset reanalysis", and Google Scholar "cited by" if reachable. Also search for other Röseler anchoring papers 2023–2026 (e.g., via OpenAlex author filter: find Lukas Röseler's author ID with https://api.openalex.org/authors?search=Lukas%20R%C3%B6seler then works?filter=author.id:<id>,publication_year:2022-2026) — list all anchoring-related ones and note any that analyse anchor distance, relative adjustment ("Absolute versus relative adjustment from anchors", Röseler & Wagner 2021, osf.io/dsyrk — find any write-up), or OpAQ reanalyses. Also check the OSF project wiki/description of ygnvb (metadata only, via https://api.osf.io/v2/nodes/ygnvb/ and its wikis/children node titles — NOT files) for listed publications using the dataset.

HARD CONSTRAINTS:
- Do NOT download or open any data file (csv, xlsx, sav, rds, data zip) from osf.io/ygnvb or any OSF component or supplement — blinding rule. Node metadata/wiki text and papers only.
- Write scratch files only as /tmp/jdmsim/scratch_nov_cit_* (unique prefix; other agents share the dir).
- OpenAlex: `set -a; source ~/.claude/api_keys.env; set +a`; the default key is out of quota today; rotate through comma-separated $OPENALEX_API_KEYS. Helper: `python3 /tmp/jdmsim/scratch_nov_oa.py cites <OpenAlexID>` / `search "<q>" "<extra filter>"` / `doi <doi>`.
- Use the download-paper skill to fetch PDFs by DOI where needed. Verify DOIs via https://api.crossref.org/works/<DOI>. Page references for numbers. Mark abstract-only info as such. Never fabricate.

Final message: a table/list of all citing works found (source: OpenAlex/S2/web), each classified REUSED-OPAQ / CITED-ONLY, with a 2–4 sentence summary and page-referenced key numbers for the relevant ones; plus the list of Röseler anchoring papers 2023–2026 with status (preprint/published, DOI).

- agy-delegate: Run a prompt through the agy (Antigravity) CLI non-interactively — Gemini 3.x models for large-context reads (huge files, PDFs, logs, datasets that would bloat Claude context) and cross-model second opinions. Use whenever the task says to ask Gemini/Antigravity/agy, get a non-Claude second opinion, digest a very large file without loading it, or when you are a relay agent in a workflow instructed to pass a payload prompt through this skill.
- browser-use: Automates browser interactions for web testing, form filling, screenshots, and data extraction. Use when the user needs to navigate websites, interact with web pages, fill forms, take screenshots, or extract information from web pages.
- check-claim: Verify a specific claim attributed to an academic paper by downloading the PDF and checking the source text. Use when you need to verify whether a citation accurately represents what the paper says. Pass the DOI and the claim to verify as arguments.
- coarse-review: Produce a rigorous academic peer review of a research paper, manuscript, or preprint (PDF, markdown, TeX, DOCX, HTML, or EPUB) using the full coarse pipeline with the user's local Claude Code subscription doing all the LLM reasoning. Every pipeline stage — structure analysis, overview synthesis, per-section review, proof verification, editorial pass — is served by a headless `claude -p` subprocess instead of a paid API. Use when the user asks to review, critique, referee, or provide feedback on an academic paper. Takes 10-25 minutes. Do NOT use for code review, blog posts, or non-academic documents.
- codex-browser: Drive the user's real Chrome — signed-in sessions, cross-origin iframes, dialogs a page-injecting tool cannot reach — by delegating to the codex CLI's Chrome plugin. Use for UI work that has no API behind it, when the user asks for it, or when Claude's own mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools fail to activate a control. Not for anything an API or CLI can do.
- codex-delegate: Run a prompt through the OpenAI Codex CLI non-interactively and return its answer — for independent second opinions, code reviews, and self-contained implementation tasks delegated to codex. Use whenever the task says to get a codex opinion/review, run something through codex, delegate implementation to codex, or when you are a relay agent in a workflow instructed to pass a payload prompt through this skill. For driving the user's real Chrome, use the codex-browser skill instead.
- deploy-html: Publish a standalone HTML document (report, plan, findings, mock) to a live public URL on surge.sh, normally with the html-comments review layer switched on. Use only when the user asks for it to be deployed, published, put online, or given a link for OTHER people. Not for a throwaway / local / single-reviewer markup (that is html-comments local mode, no upload), not for a full website, and not for HTML shipped to users.
- diagnosing-bugs: Diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions. Use when the user says "diagnose"/"debug this", or reports something broken/throwing/failing/slow.
- distribute-skill: Transfer a skill to the openclaw box and make its single repository copy available to Codex, Claude Code, and OpenClaw. Use when asked to install or update a skill on the box.
- docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.
- download-paper: Download academic PDFs by DOI for claim verification. Use when you need to read/verify the content of an academic paper and have its DOI. Downloads through the fetchpdf open-access chain (Unpaywall, PMC, preprint servers, repositories), a Google Scholar step, and the user's real signed-in Chrome for paywalled sources, checking every PDF against the requested DOI.
- frontend-design: Guidance for distinctive, intentional visual design when building new UI or reshaping an existing one. Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that don't read as templated defaults.
- gdoc-comments: Add inline comments to a Google Doc from HTML comments (<!-- COMMENT/TODO/DISCUSSION -->) in a local markdown file. Use when the user wants to transfer comments from a local manuscript to a Google Doc. Preferred approach is docx with comments, with browser automation as fallback. Works on macOS only.
- grilling: Grill the user relentlessly about a plan, decision, or idea. Use when the user wants to stress-test their thinking, or uses any 'grill' trigger phrases.
- gsheet-collect-endpoint: HTTP contract for the FORRT shared Google Apps Script endpoint that appends rows to a Google Sheet (one tab per `project`) and returns per-item vote tallies. Use local mode for one reviewer's private markup in the browser, or shared mode for several reviewers and persistent comments. proposal text, evaluates each section against criteria, and outputs

- revealjs-slide-comments: Use when enabling or working with the reusable slide-comments overlay for Reveal.js HTML decks, including launching the local server, inspecting comment sidecars, applying comments from a deck, handling pasted-image comments, and preserving data-cid anchors.

- revise-with-feedback: Revise a draft passage through cross-model review — GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 3.8 Flash review it against its content and Lukas's style guide, Claude Opus 5.5 revises, and content ambiguities come back as questions instead of guesses. - teaching-review: Review audience-facing teaching / workshop / talk material: slide decks,  resource webpages, handouts, worksheets, for the failure modes of (AI)-drafted material. Three passes: VOICE & FRAMING, ACCURACY & EVIDENCE, FORM & FUNCTION.  Produces one ranked, location-specific findings report and verifies factual claims. # About me

I am Lukas, a social psychologist, meta-scientist and open science advocate, who mostly uses you to get research done and build the tooling that supports it (in addition to teaching support). I have a solid understanding of software development and infrastructure, but am no expert, so that I will often need clear recommendations and explanations. Most of what I build is tooling for one-off projects, most is not intended to be production-ready or backwards-compatible. Feel free to clarify that project-by-project, but generally lean, efficient and clear code is more important than any backwards-compatible shim or edge-case handling.

I also regularly need your help in writing. For that, and in code, the most annoying failure mode is when history leaks in - when a text argues against its previous versions, or code comments are more about what is gone than about what the curent code does. Here, writing and reviewing outputs from the perspective of a new reader is essential.

# How to work

## Delegation: Fable as Orchestrator

When the session model is Fable, work **orchestrator-first**: plan, delegate substantive work to cheaper subagents, then review and synthesize. Fable itself keeps task decomposition, design decisions and judgment calls, reviewing subagent output, final synthesis and user-facing writing, plus edits so trivial that delegating would take longer. Everything else — implementation, broad searches, analyses, mechanical batch work — goes to subagents by default.

## Using sub-agents

- **Default subagent model: Opus** (`model: "opus"` on the Agent tool / workflow `agent()` calls). Drop to Sonnet or Haiku for clearly mechanical, high-volume steps; reserve Fable-model subagents for only the hardest verify/judge stages.
- **codex CLI** — via the `codex-delegate` skill: (a) independent second opinions and code review (read-only), and (b) self-contained implementation tasks with `--approve-for-me` — good for parallel, independent work streams.
- **agy CLI** (Antigravity; Gemini 3.x + others, `agy models` lists them) — via the `agy-delegate` skill: (a) **large-context reads** — digesting big files, PDFs, logs, or datasets that would bloat Claude context — and (b) **cross-model second opinions**.
- **In Workflow scripts**, reach codex/agy through cheap relay agents: `agent(relayPrompt, {model: 'sonnet', effort: 'low'})`, where `relayPrompt` says "You are a relay agent. Pass the following payload prompt through the `codex-delegate` [or `agy-delegate`] skill, wait for its answer, and return its answer verbatim as your final message; do not answer the payload yourself." followed by the payload, the working directory, and mode/model choices. The relay is pure transport — the skill holds the CLI recipe; keep payload prompts self-contained. Make sure the agents run the request in the foreground, with generous timeout as a subagent that backgrounds codex and waits on monitors/notifications often never gets resumed, stranding the finished answer on disk. If a codex-relay subagent goes quiet, don't wait for it — `ls` for the output file and read it directly.
- Delegation must not degrade quality: give subagents complete, self-contained prompts with all needed context and file paths, and verify load-bearing results yourself rather than trusting a subagent's summary.
- Assign clear ownership of every delegated write target.   screenshot to see the state instead of reissuing the identical call. Never put
  `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(…))` inside injected JS — the CDP call itself
  then times out.

contaminate stdout. Write to a file first (`gws … --format json > out.json 2>err.log`),

print the top-level keys before indexing into them.

Keep a prose rule only when it requires judgment. State the decision and the failure mode it prevents.

## Statistical analyses

In my research, I often need your help with statistical analyses. Make sure these are appropriate and robust. If we change direction and another analysis approach becomes more appropriate, we should generally change track (unless compute cost is very high).

When reproducing, replicating, or re-analysing a previous study, match the original as faithfully as possible by DEFAULT — same sample inclusion rules, same variables, same operationalisations, same model. Do NOT introduce deviations (different year ranges, team/group-size filters, measures, controls, transformations) for convenience, tractability, or unstated preference. When a deviation is kept, state it and its justification plainly in the writeup and flag it briefly in the code.

## Status Reports and Summaries: Plain Over Clever

When reporting progress, findings, or decisions, write like a technical changelog,
not a narrated story. The test: could someone who did not watch the work act on
each sentence without rereading it or asking what it refers to? For that, largely use
ASD-STE100, but deviate where that increases clarity and readability.

Concretely:

1. **Lead with the fact, not the framing.** "Added a manifest hash check at Stage 3
   startup; hashing 300 MB takes 0.10 s" — not "The manifest binding is in,
   positioned with the other startup refusals, and the agent measured the cost
   rather than assuming it."
2. **No process narration.** Skip who suggested what, what was declined, what an
   agent "pushed back" on, and why a fix is "worth noting". Report the decision and
   its one-line reason; drop the story of how it was reached unless asked.
3. **Resolve every reference in place.** Never write "#17", "the #8 question",
   or a label coined earlier in the session without saying what
   it is: "finding #17 (rule-pick caching during outages)". Assume the reader has
   no memory of the earlier conversation.
4. **One clause, one fact.** No sentences that stack a claim, its justification,
   and a contrast with an alternative separated by dashes. Split them.
5. **Structure over prose for multi-item status.** Three or more parallel items

   with a bolded label per item, not woven into paragraphs.

   because", "the honest answer is", "notably". State the fact; let it carry its
   own weight.

   so nothing waiting on the user is buried mid-paragraph.

training. Do not dumb things down or pad explanations — just prefer the plain term
when one exists and carries the same meaning: "check before writing" over
"TOCTOU-safe", "lookup table" over "hashmap semantics", "partly overwritten file" 
over "torn write". When a term of art is genuinely the precise word (idempotent, race condition), 
use it, and add a five-word gloss in parentheses the first time it appears in a session if the
meaning isn't clear from context. Never use jargon as compression when a plain
phrase is barely longer.

- `academic/wallrich_academic_style_guide.md` — voice, spelling, hedging, banned vocabulary, sentence structure, citations, footnotes. Section-specific detail in `academic/sections/{introduction,methods,discussion}.md`. 
- `teaching/wallrich_teaching_style_guide.md` — slides, workshops, handouts, and other audience-facing material.

3. If a DOI cannot be found, **omit the DOI field** rather than inventing one.
4. For author names, titles, and publication details: verify against Crossref metadata or the publisher's website. Do not rely on memory for these details.

## Key failure mode - insufficient editing / drift

## Keys

Reusable API keys live in `~/.claude/api_keys.env` (private to this machine, never shared). Load them with `set -a; source ~/.claude/api_keys.env; set +a` before running a script that needs them. 

Holds OpenAlex keys: `OPENALEX_API_KEY` (default) and `OPENALEX_API_KEYS` (comma-separated list of all keys). Rotate when quota is exhausted.

## Model Versions

Never assume that a model version I specify does not exist just because it's newer than your training data. If you're uncertain whether a model exists, search the web to verify. Never silently substitute an older version.

## API Cost Management

CRITICAL: Before launching any substantial paid-API job (batch LLM calls, large embedding/generation runs, anything looping over many items), explicitly estimate and confirm the cost with me *before* spending:
1. **State the estimate up front**: (price per token × tokens/call × number of calls), and say it out loud before running. Get confirmation for anything beyond a few dollars.
2. **Watch reasoning/thinking models**: a thinking model bills its hidden reasoning tokens as output and can cost ~10-30× a plain model for the same task. Prefer non-thinking models when output is short (e.g. a small JSON), and cap/lower the reasoning budget when a thinking model is needed.
3. **Use the cheapest viable provider/routing**: on OpenRouter pin cheapest-provider routing WITH a performance floor — `provider: {sort: "price", preferred_min_throughput: 40}` (tok/s; `preferred_max_latency` also exists) — because a pure price sort can route to a host queuing requests for minutes each. Add `require_parameters: true` when the call needs structured output (the cheapest host for a model does not always support it). Enable prompt caching when a large prefix is reused. Use `flex` tiers with OpenAi and Gemini that offer batch pricing at the cost of higher latency.
4. **Capture actual spend**: request usage/cost in the response and report it, so estimates can be checked against reality. If a run is substantially more expensive than estimated, stop and re-confirm.

## Backward Compatibility and Tests

Only add backward-compatibility shims, fallbacks, or dual-format handling in production systems. During development, keep the code clean — delete the old format and move on. If unsure whether something needs backward compatibility, ask before adding it.

Ensure core functionality is covered by tests, but avoid slop and large sets of smoke tests. Less is more.

## Make Reruns Safe

For every command, lifecycle step, or processing loop that may be retried, restarted, or interrupted, design it to reach the correct end state after any number of runs. This includes file-writing scripts and batched external calls.

Check two cases: a second run after success, and a run after interruption at each step. If a prior run may have left partial or stale state, inspect it before continuing. Reuse completed work, repair incomplete outputs, and remove artifacts or locks only after confirming that they are stale.

When deciding whether work is complete, compare stable content or identifiers, not file count or creation order.

## Commands For Me To Run: Copy-Pasteable, Never Illustrative

Any command written for me to run should work as-is when pasted into my shell from the
project root. No placeholders I have to resolve, and no interpreter or tool that is
not on my PATH — I copy what you write and run it.

In practice this means naming the project's own interpreter or entry point rather than
a generic one: `.venv/bin/python -m extract.export --release abc123`, not
`python -m extract.export ...`.

## Verification Before Finishing

Always verify that changes work (run tests, render outputs, check results) before presenting them as complete. Don't leave the user with "to verify, do X" — do it yourself.

When modifying code that produces visual output (plots, charts, UI components), always render and visually inspect the result before presenting the change as complete. Never declare formatting fixes "done" based on code logic alone, except for internal-facing HTML pages. For these, trust your judgement.

When editing something that is deployed (e.g. a GH page), deploying it is part of the task. When the edit is trivial, deploy. When it needs my review, ask for confirmation - but never let me guess whether the latest update is live.

# Working with git

## Committing: Fetch Before Building a Commit Stack

`git fetch` and check `main...origin/main` BEFORE committing, especially when building a stack. 
Also check `git log` for local commits that appeared since the session started (a collaborator or another session may have committed from the same checkout); verify shared files weren't clobbered before stacking on top.

## Parallel Agents in Git Worktrees

- **Merge by the agent's merge-base, never against current main/master.** An agent branches from
  the state that existed when it started, so `git diff main <branch>` carries *deletions of
  everything merged since*; applying it silently reverts already-merged work, with nothing in the
  output to indicate it. Use
  `git diff $(git merge-base main <branch>) <branch> -- <file>` to get only the agent's own
  changes, and re-verify previously merged work after each merge — not just the piece just landed.
- **Remove each worktree as it lands, not at the end.** Each is a full checkout; a wide wave can
  fill the disk mid-session, and worktree creation then fails with "No space left on device".

  and `grep --include=*.html` abort with `no matches found` when nothing matches.
  Quote globs passed as arguments (`--include='*.html'`); guard optional ones
  (`ls foo* 2>/dev/null || true`).

## Chrome Extension: Local Files, Tabs, Busy Pages

- The extension cannot open `file://` URLs. To view local HTML, serve the directory
  (`python3 -m http.server <port>`, backgrounded) and open
  `http://localhost:<port>/<file>`.
- Never reuse a tabId from an earlier turn or session; call tabs_context_mcp for
  live IDs after any tab error. Don't make navigate the first action of a
  browser_batch — create the tab first.
- If a screenshot/scroll/javascript call times out, the page is mid-load: take one
  screenshot to see the state instead of reissuing the identical call. Never put
  `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(…))` inside injected JS — the CDP call itself
  then times out.

## Google Workspace

For any Google Workspace task (Docs, Sheets, Drive, Gmail, Calendar, Slides, Forms), use the `gws` CLI (`/opt/homebrew/bin/gws`). Discover the API with `gws <service> --help` and `gws schema <service.resource.method>`. Fall back to browser automation only for things gws cannot do, such as viewing rendered output.

Never pipe `gws` output directly into a JSON parser: keyring warnings and preamble
contaminate stdout. Write to a file first (`gws … --format json > out.json 2>err.log`),
`head -c 300` it to confirm it is JSON, then parse. Pass API arguments through
`--params '<JSON>'`, not as flags or positionals. After parsing any API response,
print the top-level keys before indexing into them.

## Sanity-Check Prompts

If a user prompt seems unrelated to the current project/working directory, or references files, concepts, or protocols that don't exist in the codebase, ask the user to confirm before proceeding. They may be in the wrong folder.

## Scratch / Throwaway Files

Name temporary or throwaway files with a `scratch` prefix (e.g. `scratch.py`, `scratch_notes.md`, `scratch_test.js`). The `/wrap` end-of-session skill detects files matching `scratch*` and offers to commit or delete them during wrap-up.

## Recurring Corrections Become Mechanisms

When the same correction or unexpected failure recurs, encode the fix in a mechanism: a test, hook, lint rule, validation step, safer code default, or automation. Apply the mechanism now and remove the duplicate prose.

Use the strongest mechanism available. Prefer a restriction that makes an invalid state impossible. If that is not possible, use a lint or CI check, a shared helper, or a runtime check.

Keep a prose rule only when it requires judgment. State the decision and the failure mode it prevents.

## Statistical analyses

In my research, I often need your help with statistical analyses. Make sure these are appropriate and robust. If we change direction and another analysis approach becomes more appropriate, we should generally change track (unless compute cost is very high).

### Reproducing / Replicating Prior Analyses

When reproducing, replicating, or re-analysing a previous study, match the original as faithfully as possible by DEFAULT — same sample inclusion rules, same variables, same operationalisations, same model. Do NOT introduce deviations (different year ranges, team/group-size filters, measures, controls, transformations) for convenience, tractability, or unstated preference. If a deviation is genuinely warranted (e.g. to fix a confound, handle censoring, or reduce compute), STOP and flag it explicitly, explain why, and get agreement before building on it. When a deviation is kept, state it and its justification plainly in the writeup and flag it briefly in the code.

# Writing

## Status Reports and Summaries: Plain Over Clever

When reporting progress, findings, or decisions, write like a technical changelog,
not a narrated story. The test: could someone who did not watch the work act on
each sentence without rereading it or asking what it refers to? For that, largely use
ASD-STE100, but deviate where that increases clarity and readability.

Concretely:

1. **Lead with the fact, not the framing.** "Added a manifest hash check at Stage 3
   startup; hashing 300 MB takes 0.10 s" — not "The manifest binding is in,
   positioned with the other startup refusals, and the agent measured the cost
   rather than assuming it."
2. **No process narration.** Skip who suggested what, what was declined, what an
   agent "pushed back" on, and why a fix is "worth noting". Report the decision and
   its one-line reason; drop the story of how it was reached unless asked.
3. **Resolve every reference in place.** Never write "#17", "the #8 question",
   or a label coined earlier in the session without saying what
   it is: "finding #17 (rule-pick caching during outages)". Assume the reader has
   no memory of the earlier conversation.
4. **One clause, one fact.** No sentences that stack a claim, its justification,
   and a contrast with an alternative separated by dashes. Split them.
5. **Structure over prose for multi-item status.** Three or more parallel items
   (fixes applied, decisions pending, open questions) go in a list or short table
   with a bolded label per item, not woven into paragraphs.
6. **Ban editorializing connectors**: "which is the entire point", "worth noting
   because", "the honest answer is", "notably". State the fact; let it carry its
   own weight.
7. **Separate done / pending / needs-my-decision** into visibly distinct blocks,
   so nothing waiting on the user is buried mid-paragraph.

## Jargon: I Know the Concepts, Not the Vocabulary

I have a solid working understanding of programming and systems, but no formal CS
training. Do not dumb things down or pad explanations — just prefer the plain term
when one exists and carries the same meaning: "check before writing" over
"TOCTOU-safe", "lookup table" over "hashmap semantics", "partly overwritten file" 
over "torn write". When a term of art is genuinely the precise word (idempotent, race condition), 
use it, and add a five-word gloss in parentheses the first time it appears in a session if the
meaning isn't clear from context. Never use jargon as compression when a plain
phrase is barely longer.

## Style Guides

My written style guides live in `~/Documents/Coding/style_guides`:

- `academic/wallrich_academic_style_guide.md` — voice, spelling, hedging, banned vocabulary, sentence structure, citations, footnotes. Section-specific detail in `academic/sections/{introduction,methods,discussion}.md`. 
- `teaching/wallrich_teaching_style_guide.md` — slides, workshops, handouts, and other audience-facing material.

Read the relevant guide before drafting, revising, or reviewing my prose in that register, and before proposing additions to it.

## Statistical Results in Quarto/Rmd Reports

CRITICAL: NEVER write interpretive prose about statistical results you haven't seen. Produce the numbers first, read the rendered output, then write the text. The full conventions are in the `quarto-reporting` skill. Load it when creating or editing `.qmd` or `.Rmd` files.

## Academic References and DOIs

CRITICAL: NEVER fabricate DOIs, citation metadata, or reference details from memory. DOIs, author lists, titles, page numbers, and volume/issue numbers are exact identifiers — getting them wrong is worse than omitting them.

When creating references:
1. **Always look up DOIs** via the Crossref API (`https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic={url_encoded_reference}`) or web search. Never guess a DOI.
2. **Verify each DOI resolves** by fetching `https://api.crossref.org/works/{DOI}` and checking the returned metadata matches.
3. If a DOI cannot be found, **omit the DOI field** rather than inventing one.
4. For author names, titles, and publication details: verify against Crossref metadata or the publisher's website. Do not rely on memory for these details.

## Reading Academic Articles from HTML

When reading an academic article from an HTML page, ensure the page has fully loaded before extracting or searching its text, and confirm you are actually looking at the full text rather than just the abstract/landing view. A search that comes back empty can mean the content hasn't rendered yet, not that it isn't there. Take a screenshot to see what is actually on the page, before concluding a section is missing or treating the abstract as the whole article.

## Key failure mode - insufficient editing / drift

### The text has no memory of its drafts

Readers see only the final text, never its revision history. They do not know what an earlier draft said, what was wrong with it, or why a claim was softened or dropped. All external writing must read as a clean, self-contained statement of the *current* message, not as a reply to a previous version. Watch for "history leakage": phrasing that only makes sense against a framing the reader never saw. Tells include "not simply X", "rather than Y", "this is not the wrong variable", "to be fair", "the honest limits are narrower", "less a reprieve than a reminder", "we no longer…", and defensive hedges that rebut objections raised only in our own discussion. State the positive claim directly — say what the thing IS and what genuinely limits it, not what it is not relative to a draft.

This applies with full force to durable reference text: CLAUDE.md rules, code comments, docs, commit messages, skill files. A rule states the current fact ("GNU coreutils is on PATH"), never the story of its own correction — no "installed Jul 2026", "exists now", "no longer missing", "fixed since", "never assume X is absent". Those phrasings only make sense to someone who held the old, wrong belief; every future reader starts from the rule itself. Before saving any rule or comment, reread it as a stranger: if it reads as a rebuttal, rewrite it as the fact.

### When we agree to restructure, actually restart

If you and I agree to write a *fresh* draft or a new outline rather than edit the existing one, write it fresh from the agreed outline. Do not silently carry over the previous version's spine, ordering, emphasis, or lead just because it's already there — that is how an obsolete framing survives a "rewrite." Carry over only the verified facts, numbers and sources; treat the prior draft's structure as superseded unless we explicitly decide to keep a part of it.

# HTML files as a common output

Whenever you write long plans, proposals or report, assume HTML output as a default. It is more readable than md. When you need detailed feedback, include */html-comments*.

Link identifiers wherever they resolve: DOIs as `https://doi.org/…`, arXiv IDs as `https://arxiv.org/abs/…`, repos, issues, dataset accessions. Cited constructs (a named statistic, rubric or method) get a short hover gloss (`<abbr title="…">`) and a References section at the end.

Every standalone HTML file gets an emoji favicon as a `data:` URI, right after `<title>`:

```html
<link rel="icon" href="data:image/svg+xml,<svg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' viewBox='0 0 100 100'><text y='.9em' font-size='90'>🦸</text></svg>">
```

- Pick for the page's **topic**, never its type (no 📋 for every plan, 📊 for every
  report) — several are open at once and must be distinguishable. Keep it stable
  across edits to a file.
- Escape `#` as `%23`; keep double quotes outside, single quotes inside.
- Safari ignores SVG favicons: for participant- or reviewer-facing pages use
  `type="image/png"` with a base64 PNG (`base64 -i icon.png | tr -d '\n'`).

To open a webpage for the user, use the Bash tool to run `open <url>`. Do not use Claude artefacts by default. Keep scratch files local, deploy single collaborative files to surge.sh, and use GH pages for project-related files that are supposed to be shared.

# Working with APIs

## Keys

Reusable API keys live in `~/.claude/api_keys.env` (private to this machine, never shared). Load them with `set -a; source ~/.claude/api_keys.env; set +a` before running a script that needs them. 

Holds OpenAlex keys: `OPENALEX_API_KEY` (default) and `OPENALEX_API_KEYS` (comma-separated list of all keys). Rotate when quota is exhausted.

## Model Versions

Never assume that a model version I specify does not exist just because it's newer than your training data. If you're uncertain whether a model exists, search the web to verify. Never silently substitute an older version.

## API Cost Management

CRITICAL: Before launching any substantial paid-API job (batch LLM calls, large embedding/generation runs, anything looping over many items), explicitly estimate and confirm the cost with me *before* spending:
1. **State the estimate up front**: (price per token × tokens/call × number of calls), and say it out loud before running. Get confirmation for anything beyond a few dollars.
2. **Watch reasoning/thinking models**: a thinking model bills its hidden reasoning tokens as output and can cost ~10-30× a plain model for the same task. Prefer non-thinking models when output is short (e.g. a small JSON), and cap/lower the reasoning budget when a thinking model is needed.
3. **Use the cheapest viable provider/routing**: on OpenRouter pin cheapest-provider routing WITH a performance floor — `provider: {sort: "price", preferred_min_throughput: 40}` (tok/s; `preferred_max_latency` also exists) — because a pure price sort can route to a host queuing requests for minutes each. Add `require_parameters: true` when the call needs structured output (the cheapest host for a model does not always support it). Enable prompt caching when a large prefix is reused. Use `flex` tiers with OpenAi and Gemini that offer batch pricing at the cost of higher latency.
4. **Capture actual spend**: request usage/cost in the response and report it, so estimates can be checked against reality. If a run is substantially more expensive than estimated, stop and re-confirm.

# Coding practices

## Backward Compatibility and Tests

Only add backward-compatibility shims, fallbacks, or dual-format handling in production systems. During development, keep the code clean — delete the old format and move on. If unsure whether something needs backward compatibility, ask before adding it.

Ensure core functionality is covered by tests, but avoid slop and large sets of smoke tests. Less is more.

## Make Reruns Safe

For every command, lifecycle step, or processing loop that may be retried, restarted, or interrupted, design it to reach the correct end state after any number of runs. This includes file-writing scripts and batched external calls.

Check two cases: a second run after success, and a run after interruption at each step. If a prior run may have left partial or stale state, inspect it before continuing. Reuse completed work, repair incomplete outputs, and remove artifacts or locks only after confirming that they are stale.

When deciding whether work is complete, compare stable content or identifiers, not file count or creation order.

## Commands For Me To Run: Copy-Pasteable, Never Illustrative

Any command written for me to run should work as-is when pasted into my shell from the
project root. No placeholders I have to resolve, and no interpreter or tool that is
not on my PATH — I copy what you write and run it.

In practice this means naming the project's own interpreter or entry point rather than
a generic one: `.venv/bin/python -m extract.export --release abc123`, not
`python -m extract.export ...`.

## Verification Before Finishing

Always verify that changes work (run tests, render outputs, check results) before presenting them as complete. Don't leave the user with "to verify, do X" — do it yourself.

When modifying code that produces visual output (plots, charts, UI components), always render and visually inspect the result before presenting the change as complete. Never declare formatting fixes "done" based on code logic alone, except for internal-facing HTML pages. For these, trust your judgement.

When editing something that is deployed (e.g. a GH page), deploying it is part of the task. When the edit is trivial, deploy. When it needs my review, ask for confirmation - but never let me guess whether the latest update is live.

# Working with git

## Committing: Fetch Before Building a Commit Stack

`git fetch` and check `main...origin/main` BEFORE committing, especially when building a stack. 
Also check `git log` for local commits that appeared since the session started (a collaborator or another session may have committed from the same checkout); verify shared files weren't clobbered before stacking on top.

## Parallel Agents in Git Worktrees

- **Merge by the agent's merge-base, never against current main/master.** An agent branches from
  the state that existed when it started, so `git diff main <branch>` carries *deletions of
  everything merged since*; applying it silently reverts already-merged work, with nothing in the
  output to indicate it. Use
  `git diff $(git merge-base main <branch>) <branch> -- <file>` to get only the agent's own
  changes, and re-verify previously merged work after each merge — not just the piece just landed.
- **Remove each worktree as it lands, not at the end.** Each is a full checkout; a wide wave can
  fill the disk mid-session, and worktree creation then fails with "No space left on device".

import json, os, sys, urllib.request, urllib.parse
keys = [k.strip() for k in os.environ['OPENALEX_API_KEYS'].split(',') if k.strip()]
def get(url):
    for k in keys:
        u = url + ('&' if '?' in url else '?') + 'api_key=' + k
        try:
            d = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(u, timeout=60))
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
            d = json.loads(e.read() or b'{}')
        if 'error' not in d: return d
    raise SystemExit('all keys exhausted: ' + str(d)[:200])

    for w in d['results']:

elif mode == 'search':

Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type parameter to select which agent type to use. If omitted, the general-purpose agent is used.

## When to use

Reach for this when the task matches an available agent type, when you have independent work to run in parallel, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate it and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps. For a single-fact lookup where you already know the file, symbol, or value, search directly. Once you've delegated a search, don't also run it yourself — wait for the result.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.

- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

<system-reminder>
# MCP Server Instructions

The following MCP servers have provided instructions for how to use their tools and resources:

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>\n\n<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>\n\n<?claude block s1?>\n\n<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder>
While bypass permissions mode is active:

You can do much of your work through the Bash tool when it is the simpler route: read files with cat, head, or sed -n, search with grep and find, and make small, mechanical file changes with sed, heredocs, or short scripts instead of the dedicated Read, Edit, or Write tools. The choice is yours: prefer Edit or Write when a shell edit would be fragile, such as exact or multi-line replacements, or sed/awk flags that differ between GNU and BSD/macOS.
</system-reminder>

  abstract: After considering a more or less random number (i.e., an anchor), people’s subsequent estimates are biased toward that number. Such anchoring phenomena have been explained via an adjustment process that ends too early. We present a formalized version of the insufficient adjustment model, which captures the idea that decreasing the time that people have to adjust from anchors draws their estimates closer to the anchors. In four independent studies (N = 898), we could not confirm this effect of time on anchoring. Moreover, anchoring effects vanished in the two studies that deviated from classical paradigms by using a visual scale or a two-alternative forced-choice paradigm to allow faster responses. Although we propose that the current version of the insufficient adjustment model should be discarded, we believe that adjustment models hold the most potential for the future of anchoring research, and we make suggestions for what these might look like.

  abstract: Although anchoring research has explored personality moderators for at least 13 years, it has not produced any robust findings. The reason for this surprising fact is rooted in the problem that most anchoring tasks have unacceptable reliability levels. In a preregistered experiment, we introduce a paradigm that we call the stepwise anchoring paradigm. It is based on the incumbent insufficient adjustment model of anchoring and previous research by Frech et al. (2020). Using the stepwise anchoring paradigm and estimates of animals’ weights, we reliably measured parameters of anchoring effects and investigated whether these parameters were correlated with theoretically relevant personality traits (i.e., cognitive reflection and impulsiveness). The reliability of the number of adjustment steps was acceptable (α = .869, 12 items, N = 125) and much higher than the reliability of the total adjustment (α = .387), which has previously been used as an indicator of susceptibility to anchoring. However, we found no robust anchoring effects and no correlations between anchoring parameters and impulsivity or cognitive reflection. Thus, although a method for reliably measuring the susceptibility to anchoring is now available, its validity is still questionable.

# ygnvb The Open Anchoring Quest (OpAQ) | The OpAQ is an ever-growing, free, open, multi-study, item-level dataset that allows researchers to solve current challenges in anchoring effects research. | 2023-11-22T16:18:48.075558
  WIKI home
   [![OPAQ][1]][2]

**What is [OpAQ][3]?**

Research on anchoring effects is currently challenged by the lack of reliability of anchoring scores, a large amount of heterogeneity between anchoring effect sizes, and by numerous contradictory findings. With OpAQ, we try to solve these problems by providing an open, free, and ever-growing dataset already containing thousands of trials from several studies on anchoring effects.


**What are your benefits of joining us?**

You are very welcome to contribute data from your anchoring experiment(s)! In return, (apart from being rewarded by the good feeling of helping research on anchoring effects to improve) we will list you as a contributor on the OpAQ website. If you send us your data, we can convert it and add it to the OpAQ dataset. You can also use our data curation template and convert your data yourself. Accordingly, we will mention your contribution either as “Resources” or additionally as “Data curation”.

Unpublished datasets as well as data from classroom experiments are also highly appreciated.


**What can you do with the OpAQ dataset?**

The OpAQ dataset can be accessed and downloaded via our ShinyApp (https://metaanalyses.shinyapps.io/OpAQ/) or our OSF project (https://osf.io/ygnvb/).

In our [ShinyApp][4], you can explore the dataset and the dynamic meta-analysis on anchoring effect sizes and the reliabilities of anchoring susceptibility scores. The dataset also provides the opportunity to test additional hypotheses, such as file-drawer-effects, effects of anchor extremeness, or age effects.

In the [OSF project][5], you can find further information and files on our project. There, you also can send us a contribution request to the project (make sure to also send us an e-mail after you requested access).

**What does the OpAQ dataset look like?**

The OpAQ dataset is an item-based dataset with a row for every single estimation of all the anchoring items it contains. For every estimate, different variables and anchoring scores are specified. We also provide a [text file][6] with descriptions of all variables that are included in the dataset.
For questions, please send an e-mail to lukas.roeseler(at)uni-bamberg.de

**I noticed an error in the dataset, what should I do?**

Please notify us about the error using the [error notification form][7],

  [2]: https://metaanalyses.shinyapps.io/OpAQ/

  [4]: https://metaanalyses.shinyapps.io/OpAQ/
  [5]: http://OSF%20project
  [6]: https://osf.io/j2xmt/

Base directory for this skill: ~/.claude/skills/download-paper

# Download & Verify Academic Papers

`$SKILL_DIR` below is wherever this skill lives (e.g. `~/.claude/skills/download-paper`).

## Step 1: Try downloading the PDF

```bash
PDF_PATH=$($SKILL_DIR/download_paper.py --doi "DOI_HERE" 2>/tmp/download_paper.log)
```

Run the script directly — its shebang is `uv run --script`, which installs
[`fetchpdf`](https://github.com/The-Metascience-Observatory/fetchpdf) into a managed
environment on first use (a few seconds); later runs reuse uv's cache. The fetchpdf version
is pinned to a commit hash in the script's `# dependencies` header; edit that hash to update.

Sources, in order:

1. Cache (a copy of this DOI fetched earlier)
2. The fetchpdf open-access chain: OpenAlex, Unpaywall, PubMed Central, Europe PMC,
   Crossref links, Semantic Scholar, arXiv and other preprint servers, repository
   landing pages, publisher routes
3. Google Scholar via SerpAPI
4. The user's running, signed-in Chrome — one throwaway tab walks the Scholar links plain
   HTTP could not fetch, then the publisher's own PDF URLs (canonical URL by DOI prefix,
   `citation_pdf_url` from the landing page, ScienceDirect `/pdfft`), then EBSCOhost

Every downloaded PDF is checked against the requested DOI, title and page range. A
different paper, or a publisher preview of only the first page, is discarded and the walk
moves on to the next candidate.

**What the Chrome step needs** (it logs one line and skips when any of these is missing):

- macOS, with Google Chrome already running and at least one window open
- Chrome signed in to the publisher or EBSCO through the user's institution / OpenAthens
- *View ▸ Developer ▸ Allow JavaScript from Apple Events* switched on once
- `INSTITUTION_EBSCO_PROFILE` set to the library's EBSCO cluster id, for the EBSCO candidate

The step opens its tab at the end of the front window, never focuses it, and closes it
again on the way out, so it does not disturb what the user is doing.

Options:

- `--title "Paper Title"` — the Google Scholar query; otherwise taken from Crossref
- `--force` — re-download even if cached
- `--no-browser` — skip the Chrome step (leaves the run entirely non-interactive)
- `--playwright` — let fetchpdf render JS-heavy pages in a headless browser. Slower, and
  Cloudflare-protected publishers block it, so it is off by default.
- `--open` — on failure, open the best candidate URL in the user's browser for manual download

Exit codes: 0 = success (path on stdout), 1 = failure, 2 = opened in browser for manual download.

## Step 2: Read the downloaded PDF

```bash
pdftotext "$PDF_PATH" - | head -200           # First 200 lines
pdftotext "$PDF_PATH" - | grep -A5 "keyword"  # Search for specific claims
```

## Step 3: When the download fails

The script lists its candidate URLs on stderr, each with a note:

1. `[Scholar link, no PDF by plain HTTP]` — a PDF link Google Scholar offered that returned
   403, a bot check, or a landing page. The Chrome step tries these first when it runs.
2. `[Scholar link, a different paper]` — fetched, but not this DOI's paper. Skip it.
3. `[publisher page]` — `https://doi.org/DOI_HERE`, which honours institutional access

Three manual routes, in the order worth trying.

### 3a: Sign in at this publisher, then re-run

One OpenAthens handshake covers one publisher. A login at publisher A does not
authenticate publisher B, and the Chrome step can only use sessions that already exist.
Ask the user to open the `[publisher page]` URL, click *Access through your institution*,
and say when they are through; then re-run Step 1 with `--force`.

### 3b: Read the paper off the page

When no PDF exists to download (a landing page with the full text in HTML, an
Academia.edu or ResearchGate record), read the content instead. `browser-use --browser
real` drives the user's Chrome and returns structured page content — abstract, key
findings, figure captions, references — which is often enough for claim verification.

```bash
uvx browser-use --browser real open "PAPER_URL"
uvx browser-use state          # structured page content; repeat after `scroll down`
uvx browser-use close          # always close when done
```

`browser-use` is unreliable against heavy JS apps such as the EBSCO viewer: `state` and
`eval` come back empty there. Use it for ordinary publisher pages.

### 3c: Run one route on its own

`institutional_fetch.py` holds the Chrome layer Step 1 uses, and its CLI runs a single
route against one DOI — useful for debugging a route or for the cookie-jar route, which
Step 1 does not use.

```bash
$SKILL_DIR/institutional_fetch.py --doi "10.1037/edu0000827" --ebsco 2>/tmp/inst.log
$SKILL_DIR/institutional_fetch.py --doi "..." --ebsco --all-db   # beyond PsycInfo
$SKILL_DIR/institutional_fetch.py export-cookies                 # once, after logging in
$SKILL_DIR/institutional_fetch.py --doi "10.1080/..." 2>/tmp/inst.log   # cookie-jar route
```

Success prints the verified PDF's path on stdout (same contract as `download_paper.py`).

### Critical gotchas (learned the hard way)

- **Verify page 1 against the DOI or title for anything you fetch by hand.** Title-based
  search returns topically-similar papers under the DOI you asked for, and a mislabelled
  PDF silently corrupts whatever dataset it lands in. `download_paper.py` and
  `institutional_fetch.py` both run fetchpdf's identity check themselves; the `browser-use`
  route does not.
- **Navigate before you fetch.** Cross-origin fetch of a publisher PDF is CORS-blocked. The
  Chrome step navigates the tab to the PDF URL first, waits until
  `document.contentType == 'application/pdf'`, then fetches same-origin with credentials —
  the asset host (`pdf.sciencedirectassets.com`, silverchair, `content.ebscohost.com`) is
  same-origin once the tab is on it. The wait also lets Cloudflare, Anubis and Imperva
  interstitials clear themselves, which they do in a real browser and never under curl.
- **Chrome's PDF viewer cannot return a Promise to AppleScript.** The in-page fetch parks
  its base64 on `window.__pdf`; a poll collects it and reads it back in 800k-character
  chunks. A plain `return await fetch(...)` yields an empty string with no error.
- **Chrome's AppleScript tab `id` compares as a string.** `if (id of tt as string) is "…"`
  matches; a numeric `=` matches nothing and every command silently does nothing.
- **`Content-Disposition: attachment` URLs never reach the viewer.** Chrome drops the file
  in `~/Downloads` and the tab stays put, so the wait times out. Prefer the inline PDF URL
  of a pair (`/doi/pdf/…` over `/doi/pdfdirect/…?download=true`).
- **Signed EBSCO content URLs need no cookies.** `content.ebscohost.com/cds/retrieve?content=<token>`
  authenticates itself; plain `curl` downloads it. Don't rebuild the cookie dance for it.
- **EBSCO failure modes are informative.** No record id means EBSCO does not index the
  paper; a record with no content URL means EBSCO has "Linked Full Text" only — a link-out
  to the publisher, not a hosted PDF.
- **Domain-aware cookies.** A real browser holds thousands of cookies. Sending all of them to
  one host returns **`400 Request Header Or Cookie Too Large`**. The cookie-jar route builds
  a per-domain `RequestsCookieJar` so requests sends only the target host's cookies.
- **Off-campus IP gating is real.** Even in a logged-in real Chrome, SAGE / Wiley / T&F / OUP
  / IOS / Springer / BMJ direct routes are frequently campus-IP-gated. EBSCO is not. Keep a
  VPN / on-campus batch list rather than retrying.
- **Expect a low yield on paywalled batches.** One real batch: 62 paywalled papers → 8
  fetched. Plan around partial coverage.
- **The EBSCO viewer changes.** If the resource-timings lookup stops finding a
  `cds/retrieve` URL, check the viewer's network tab and the
  `research.ebsco.com/api/researcher-edge-aggregator/v1/records/<id>/fulltext/pdf?...&intent=download`
  JSON endpoint before rebuilding the flow.

## Environment Variables

Keys are read from the environment, then from `~/.claude/api_keys.env`.

- `SERPAPI_API_KEYS` (comma-separated) or `SERPAPI_API_KEY` — enables the Google Scholar
  step. Keys are tried in order; an exhausted or invalid key moves on to the next.
- `INSTITUTION_EBSCO_PROFILE` — the library's EBSCO cluster id, the `<cluster>` in the
  `research.ebsco.com/c/<cluster>/...` URL Chrome lands on after an institutional login.
  Enables the EBSCO candidate in the Chrome step.
- `CORE_API_KEY`, `ELSEVIER_API_KEY`, `OPENALEX_API_KEY` — optional; passed to fetchpdf's
  CORE, Elsevier text-mining and OpenAlex sources.
- `RESEARCHER_EMAIL` or `EMAIL` — contact address for the open-access APIs (Unpaywall
  requires one; Crossref gives a higher rate limit with one).

## Cache

Downloaded PDFs are cached in `~/.claude/cache/pdfs/` (MD5 of DOI). Use `--force` to re-download.

All available data from anchoring studies that included at least two anchors were aggregated into one large dataset, with data standardized to comprise one estimate per row and made available for download and analyses online. Because the dataset includes both original and meta-data it allows for fine-grained analyses (e.g., correlations of estimates for different tasks) but also for meta-analyses (e.g., effect sizes for anchoring effects). Here are the search results for "Falsifying the Insufficient Adjustment Model" by Röseler:

The study "Falsifying the Insufficient Adjustment Model: No Evidence for Unidirectional Adjustment from Anchors" was authored by Röseler and colleagues. It was published in Meta-Psychology, volume 9, with DOI 10.15626/MP.2024.4137.

**Key findings:**

The researchers presented a formalized version of the insufficient adjustment model and tested whether decreasing the time people have to adjust from anchors draws their estimates closer to the anchors. In four independent studies with 898 participants, they could not confirm this effect of time on anchoring.

Additionally, anchoring effects vanished in the two studies that deviated from classical paradigms by using a visual scale or a two-alternative forced-choice paradigm to allow faster responses.

The authors propose that the current version of the insufficient adjustment model should be discarded, though they believe that adjustment models hold the most potential for the future of anchoring research.

The OpAQ (Open Anchoring Quest) is an ever-growing, free, open, multi-study, item-level dataset that allows researchers to solve current challenges in anchoring effects research. The dataset includes 96 studies from 57 references, with a total sample size of 21,359 participants who provided estimates for 412 unique anchoring items, yielding a total of 88,914 trials.

## Anchoring Bias in Language Models

Research has explored how language models exhibit anchoring bias. In anchoring, a cognitive bias that both humans and large language models (LLMs) exhibit, an irrelevant number shifts a subsequent judgment, pulling estimates toward the irrelevant number. 

Recent work has studied this mechanistically using the OpAQ dataset. Researchers study anchoring bias both behaviorally and mechanistically by converting questions from the OpAQ dataset to multiple-choice format, using 100 numerical-estimation questions from OpAQ.

## Anchoring Items Structure

Each anchoring item provides a factual question, a ground-truth numerical answer, a low anchor, and a high anchor, with researchers constructing a nine-option candidate set containing the ground-truth value, the low and high anchors, and intermediate values spanning the anchor range.

Based on my web search, I found several research studies on anchoring bias in large language models. Here are the key findings:

## Main Research

Anchoring bias is a cognitive bias where initial information disproportionately influences judgment, and researchers have examined how it manifests in LLMs and tested various mitigation strategies.

## Key Findings

**Model Behavior:**
Stronger models like GPT-4 and GPT-4o are more consistently influenced by anchoring bias, while the anchoring effects are weaker on GPT-3.5. LLMs, like humans, adjust their judgments based on irrelevant numeric cues, with research replicating classic anchoring tasks using ChatGPT models.

**Mitigation Challenges:**
Researchers tested various strategies including Chain-of-Thought, Thoughts of Principles, Ignoring Anchor Hints, and Reflection to mitigate anchoring bias in LLMs, but none of these simple strategies effectively reduced the anchoring bias in responses to expert anchoring questions.

**Recommended Approaches:**
To mitigate anchoring bias, researchers suggest collecting hints from comprehensive angles to prevent LLMs from being anchored to individual pieces of information.

The search results contain multiple peer-reviewed studies on this topic, with the most recent research from late 2024 and early 2025.

                        Theories on anchoring effects—the assimilation of numerical estimates toward previ-
                        ously considered numbers—have been used to derive hypotheses that susceptibility to
                        anchoring is correlated with certain personality traits. Thus, for the last decade, a con-
                        siderable amount of research has investigated relationships between people’s suscepti-
                        bility to anchoring and personality traits (e.g., intelligence, the Big Five, narcissism).

                        is grounded in imprecise measurements. Unfortunately, few reports have disclosed
                        estimates of the susceptibility scores’ reliability (e.g., Cronbach’s Alpha or interitem
                        correlations). We created a large and open data set of anchoring susceptibility scores
                        and conducted a meta-analysis to test how extensive the reliability problem is. Results

                        After considering a more or less random number (i.e., an anchor), people’s subsequent
                        estimates are biased toward that number. Such anchoring phenomena have been ex-
                        plained via an adjustment process that ends too early. We present a formalized version
                        of the insufficient adjustment model, which captures the idea that decreasing the time
                        that people have to adjust from anchors draws their estimates closer to the anchors.
                        In four independent studies (N = 898), we could not confirm this effect of time on
                        anchoring. Moreover, anchoring effects vanished in the two studies that deviated from
                        classical paradigms by using a visual scale or a two-alternative forced-choice paradigm
                        to allow faster responses. Although we propose that the current version of the insuffi-
                        cient adjustment model should be discarded, we believe that adjustment models hold
                        the most potential for the future of anchoring research, and we make suggestions for
                        what these might look like.

                        Keywords: anchoring, TOTE, time pressure, two-alternative forced-choice, insufficient

A.1. Illustrative Empirical Demonstration
To illustrate how specification-driven variability operates in practice, we conducted a simulation examining whether
LLMs exhibit anchoring effects—the well-documented tendency in human judgment for initial numeric values to bias
subsequent estimates (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974; Jacowitz & Kahneman, 1995). Anchoring is a natural candidate for this
demonstration as it is one of the most robust and widely replicated findings in human decision-making research (Furnham &
Boo, 2011; Röseler et al., 2022).
To demonstrate how the researcher degrees of freedom involved in testing for anchoring in LLMs can generate divergent
conclusions, we constructed a full-factorial design varying specifications across the experimental pipeline. We crossed nine
models from three families (Gemini, OpenAI, Llama), three system prompt framings (human-like persona, incentivized,
none), three anchor distances (high, medium, low), three delivery methods (comparative, embedded, incidental), five
estimation questions, and two outlier-handling rules (include, exclude), yielding 2,430 unique experimental specifications.
For each specification, we computed an anchoring index, where values near zero indicate no anchoring effect and positive
values indicate that estimates were pulled toward the anchor (Jacowitz & Kahneman, 1995). Each specification represents

index from a unique combination of model family (9 models across Gemini, OpenAI, and Llama families), system prompt (human-like,

(Tversky & Kahneman, 1974; Jacowitz & Kahneman, 1995; Furnham & Boo, 2011; Röseler et al., 2022). Results span from reverse

a defensible experimental configuration—a path through the garden of forking paths that a researcher might reasonably
choose and report (Gelman & Loken, 2013).
The resulting specification curve (Figure 3) reveals substantial variability across configurations: anchoring indices range
from negative values (suggesting reverse anchoring) through zero (no effect) to values exceeding 1.0 (stronger than
effects typically observed in human studies) (Jacowitz & Kahneman, 1995; Furnham & Boo, 2011; Röseler et al., 2022).
Importantly, this variability means that a researcher’s conclusions depend heavily on which slice of the specification space
they report. A researcher selecting particular models, prompt framings, and questions could report findings consistent
with robust human-like anchoring in LLMs; a different but defensible selection could support the conclusion that LLMs
are not susceptible to anchoring at all. We emphasize that this demonstration is illustrative, not a comprehensive study
of anchoring in LLMs. We do not claim that anchoring effects in LLMs are or are not real—indeed, the point is that
the answer can depend substantially on specification choices. In other words, the space of defensible experimental

Promoting erroneous divergent opinions increases the wisdom of crowds
Federico Barrera Lermarchand1,2,3, Pablo Balenzuela2,3, Bahador Bahrami4,5,6, Ophelia Deroy7,8,9, &
Joaquin Navajas1,2,10

1 Laboratorio de Neurociencia, Universidad Torcuato Di Tella, Buenos Aires, Argentina
2 National Scientific and Technical Research Council (CONICET), Buenos Aires, Argentina
3 Departamento de Física, Facultad de Ciencias Exactas y Naturales, Universidad de Buenos Aires,
Argentina
4 Crowd Cognition Group, Department of General Psychology and Education, Ludwig Maximilian
University, Munich, Germany
5 Department of Psychology, Royal Holloway University of London, UK
6 Centre for Adaptive Rationality, Max Planck Institute for Human Development, Berlin, Germany
7 Munich Centre for Neuroscience, Ludwig Maximilian University, Munich, Germany
8 Institute of Philosophy, School of Advanced Study, University of London, London, UK
9 Faculty of Philosophy, Ludwig Maximilian University, Munich, Germany
10 Escuela de Negocios, Universidad Torcuato Di Tella, Buenos Aires, Argentina

Corresponding author: Joaquin Navajas ([email redacted])

1

 Abstract
The aggregation of many lay judgements generates surprisingly accurate estimates. This phenomenon,
called the “wisdom of crowds”, has been demonstrated in domains such as medical decision making and
financial forecasting. Previous research identified two factors driving this effect: the accuracy of
individual assessments and the diversity of opinions. Most available strategies to enhance the wisdom of
crowds have focused on improving individual accuracy while neglecting the potential of increasing
opinion diversity. Here, we study a complementary approach to reduce collective error by promoting
erroneous divergent opinions. This strategy proposes to anchor half of the crowd to a small value and the
other half to a large value before eliciting and averaging all estimates. Consistent with our mathematical
modeling, four experiments (N=1362 adults) demonstrate that this method is effective for estimation and
forecasting tasks. Beyond practical implications, these findings offer new theoretical insights into the
epistemic value of collective decision making.
Keywords: wisdom of crowds, collective intelligence, diversity, anchoring, extremization

the James McDonnell Foundation 21st Century Science Initiative in Understanding Human Cognition—
Scholar Award and by the Templeton World Charity Foundation. Ethics: This research complies with the
Declaration of Helsinki (2023) and received approval from a local ethics board (ID: 435-5).

Fig. 1. Wisdom of extremized crowds. (A) The method for estimating a variable through the wisdom of crowds
consists in asking a crowd of individuals to estimate a given quantity, and averaging all answers (averages
represented by µ). The proposed alternative method consists in promoting the adoption of divergent opinions within
a crowd by dividing it in two halves, asking an anchoring question with either a low (L) or a high (H) value to each
half, and then averaging all answers (µx). (B) Mathematical model of the anchoring effect. The anchored mean is a
weighted average of the anchor and the wisdom-of-crowds value. The weight w depends on the difference between

the anchor and the correct answer, reflecting an internal sensitivity to the correct answer. (C) Simulations performed
using the proposed model show that the method is expected to outperform the wisdom of crowds. (D) Mean
individual error and predictive diversity on simulated data show an increase in both individual error and predictive
diversity. However, the increase in individual error (left panel) is smaller than the increase in predictive diversity
(right panel), resulting in an overall reduction in collective error (“c” represents the control group, and “x” the
extremized crowd).

the mean of the original distribution of values µ. Following a variety of empirical findings linking the
anchoring effect to the plausibility of the anchor (Mussweiler & Strack, 2001; Wegener et al., 2001), we
propose that the weights 𝑤 are given by

The parameter 𝛽 is an “inverse temperature” encoding the sensitivity of the individuals to the distance
between the anchor and 𝜃. Thus, the value of 𝛽 modulates the strength of the “anchoring extremeness
effect” (Röseler et al., 2022).
In this work, we propose averaging estimates from two populations of individuals, each of which is
anchored to either a low or a high value (𝐴𝐿 or 𝐴𝐻 ). Assuming both populations are equally sized, we can

accuracy is due to an increase in diversity that surpassed the observed reduction in individual accuracy
