general tradeoff appearing under different model specifications (Fig. S1).

2. In all cases, the questions were randomly ordered (within each subset of 15 questions). In this case, we
estimated the number of participants per condition required from power analyses derived from our previous
experiment (as per our pre-registration, https://aspredicted.org/RYC_4Y5). All participants had 20 seconds
to answer the questions. Estimation was not incentivized for accuracy.
Data Analysis
For this experiment we followed the same exclusion criteria as for the previous one. In this case, the
exclusion criteria were pre-registered. For Experiment 2 we followed the same bootstrapping procedure as
stated for our previous experiment.

Results and Discussion
We observed very similar results to Experiment 1 (Fig. 3A and 3B). Collective error was lower for the
extremized crowd (crowd size N=50, unpaired t-test: t(998)=19.1, p=2x10-69; effect size: Cohen’s d = 1.2
± 0.1, 95% CL). This was accompanied by an increase in mean individual error (unpaired t-test:
t(198)=121.1, p<10-200; effect size: Cohen’s d = 7.6 ± 0.3, 95% CL) as well as an increase in predictive
diversity (unpaired t-test: t(198)=162.5, p<10-200; effect size: Cohen’s d = 10.3 ± 0.3, 95% CL).
Given that this experiment used fixed anchors across all questions, it allowed us to test one key element
of the model, i.e., the anchoring extremeness effect (Eq. [4]). We did so by performing two separate
analyses. First, we examined the biases associated with each experimental condition. We reasoned that, if
anchoring was sensitive to the distance to the correct answer, then the effectiveness of the procedure should
be higher when the correct answer is close to the anchor. For example, we should see that participants
considering a low value (5%) should be more attracted to the anchor when the correct answer is low (below

14

 50%) compared to when the correct answer is high (above 50%). Consistent with this idea, when the correct
answer was below 50% (17 questions), we did not observe any statistical difference between the
distribution of estimates provided by the population considering the “low anchor” and the correct answer,
(paired t-test, t(16)=0.95, p=.36, effect size: Cohen’s d = 0.23 ± 0.67, 95% CL), and Bayes factor analysis
provided moderate support for the null hypothesis (Bayes factor = 2.7). More importantly, both the nonanchored (paired t-test, t(16)=4.16, p=3x10-4, effect size: Cohen’s d = 1.11 ± 0.72, 95% CL) and the
population anchored to a high value (paired t-test, t(16)=5.99, p=2x10-5, effect size: Cohen’s d = 1.45 ±
0.76, 95% CL) provided a distribution of estimates that significantly overestimated the correct answer (Fig.
3C). Conversely, when the correct answer was above 50% (13 questions), we observed the opposite pattern:
the population considering the “high anchor” provided a distribution of estimates that was not statistically
distinct from the correct answer (paired t-test, t(12)=2.01, p=0.07, effect size: Cohen’s d = 0.56 ± 0.78,
95% CL), and Bayes factor analysis suggested very weak evidence in favor of the alternative hypothesis
(Bayes factor = 0.77). Crucially, both the non-anchored population (paired t-test, t(16)=3.90, p=0.001,
effect size: Cohen’s d = 1.08 ± 0.82, 95% CL) and the population anchored to a low value (paired t-test,
t(16)=4.90, p=4x10-4, effect size: Cohen’s d = 1.36 ± 0.85, 95% CL) provided a distribution of estimates
that significantly underestimated the correct answer.
Second, we directly examined the anchoring extremeness effect by studying the association between the
strength of the anchoring procedure and the distance between the anchor and the correct answer (Eq. 4).

We estimated the strength of the anchoring effect by calculating the anchoring weight, which has very
similar properties to the “anchoring index” from previous literature (Jacowitz & Kahneman, 1995). Both
quantities (see Eq. 7 in Supplementary Information for details) take a value of 0 when the anchoring
procedure does not produce any effect on the estimates, and a value of 1 when the estimates are on average
equal to the anchor. Consistent with the existence of the anchoring extremeness effect (Roseler et al., 2022),

15

 we observed a significantly negative correlation between the anchoring weight and the distance between
the anchor and the correct answer (Pearson correlation coefficient, r=-0.56, p=3x10-6). This empirical
observation provides support to the proposed model of the anchoring effect used in Eqs 2-4.
To test the functional form of the proposed model, we compared it with two other monotonically
decreasing functions. One is a linear function and the other one is a general hyperbolic function
𝑤

0
𝑤 = 1+𝛽|𝐴−𝜃|
,

[7]

which is similar to the one used in the temporal discounting literature (Ruggeri et al., 2022). We found that
the exponential model led to better fits to the data as assessed by both the Akaike and Bayesian Information
Criteria (Linear model: ∆AIC = 1.9, ∆BIC = 1.9; Hyperbolic model: ∆AIC = 0.59, ∆BIC = 0.59).
Another assumption of the proposed anchoring model is that low and high anchors elicit the same
anchoring weights. Given that this feature of the model could be an oversimplification for specific problems
(e.g., city populations), we compared the goodness of the fits achieved with a single anchoring weight per
question, with the one obtained with different weights for low and high anchors. Formal model comparison
indicated that having a single weight per question led to better fits than the model with asymmetrical
weights (∆AIC = 1.6, ∆BIC = 5.7).
Finally, this experiment allowed us testing if the proposed method is robust to the use of different
aggregation procedures like the simple average, the median, and a performance-weighted average (Mannes
et al., 2014; Collins et al, 2023). We found evidence that, regardless of the specific aggregation procedure,
crowds extremized through anchoring were always more accurate than non-extremized crowds (Fig. S3;
for details, see Supplementary Information).

content.content:
Psychonomic Bulletin & Review (2025) 32:1142–1164
https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-024-02619-9
THEORETICAL/REVIEW
Modeling dependent group judgments: A computational model
of sequential collaboration
Maren Mayer1
· Daniel W. Heck2
Accepted: 8 November 2024 / Published online: 6 January 2025
© The Author(s) 2025
Abstract
Sequential collaboration describes the incremental process of contributing to online collaborative projects such as Wikipedia
and OpenStreetMap. After a first contributor creates an initial entry, subsequent contributors create a sequential chain by
deciding whether to adjust or maintain the latest entry which is updated if they decide to make changes. Sequential collaboration
has recently been examined as a method for eliciting numerical group judgments. It was shown that in a sequential chain,
changes become less frequent and smaller, while judgments become more accurate. Judgments at the end of a sequential chain
are similarly accurate and in some cases even more accurate than aggregated independent judgments (wisdom of crowds). This
is at least partly due to sequential collaboration allowing contributors to contribute according to their expertise by selectively
adjusting judgments. However, there is no formal theory of sequential collaboration. We developed a computational model
that formalizes the cognitive processes underlying sequential collaboration. It allows modeling both sequential collaboration
and independent judgments, which are used as a benchmark for the performance of sequential collaboration. The model is
based on internal distributions of plausible judgments that contributors use to evaluate the plausibility of presented judgments
and to provide new judgments. It incorporates individuals’ expertise and tendency to adjust presented judgments as well as
item difficulty and the effects of the presented judgment on subsequent judgment formation. The model is consistent with
previous empirical findings on change probability, change magnitude, and judgment accuracy incorporating expertise as a
driving factor of these effects. Moreover, new predictions for long sequential chains were confirmed by an empirical study.
Above and beyond sequential collaboration the model establishes an initial theoretical framework for further research on
dependent judgments.

https://openalex.org/W4393006311 2024 2024-03-20 https://doi.org/10.3390/su16062540 Thermostat Anchors: Do Temperature Scale Characteristics Affect the Selection of Temperature Setpoints for Residential Homes? | authors: Torsten O. Reimer, Jeonghyun Oh, Juan Pablo Loaiza-Ramírez, Hayden Barber
  abstract: Characteristics of scales, such as the labels that are used on scales, have been shown to affect judgments. The scale-dependency hypothesis predicts specific effects of the properties of a temperature scale on residents’ choices of temperature setpoints. Based on the literature on anchoring in judgment and decision making, we assessed the effects of the displayed current temperature, midpoint, range, and increment of temperature scales on the selection of setpoint temperatures for residential homes. Participants (N = 384) were asked to imagine that they work as a manager of a residential apartment complex and to select, in this function, setpoint temperatures for incoming residents. The experiment revealed independent effects of the current temperature as well as the midpoint and range of the used scale on the selected setpoints. The scale increment did not systematically affect the chosen temperatures.
https://openalex.org/W4405719957 2024 2024-12-06 https://doi.org/10.3917/anpsy1.244.0591 Cinquante ans de travaux sur l’effet d’ancrage. Quoi de neuf depuis Tversky et Kahneman (1974) ? | authors: Aglaé Navarre, André Didierjean, Cyril Hazif Thomas
  abstract: 
https://openalex.org/W7124267073 2026 2026-01-01 https://doi.org/10.1002/bdm.70063 Information on Judgment Invariance Influences Contributors' Opting‐In Behavior in Sequential Collaboration | authors: Vincent Eric Fischer, Maren Mayer, Joachim Kimmerle
  abstract: ABSTRACT Sequential collaboration describes an aggregation process intensively researched for numerical judgments which is characterized by a first contributor creating a judgment that is subsequently adjusted or maintained by following contributors. In previous research, participants performing sequential collaboration were only provided with information about the judgment of the person immediately preceding them in a sequential chain. However, in real‐world collaborative projects (e.g., Wikipedia and Google Docs projects), more information about the past development of a sequential chain is often accessible or even directly displayed. As a concise piece of such information, we used judgment invariance, that is, the number of times a current judgment remained unchanged in the immediately preceding steps of a sequential chain. We hypothesized that increasing judgment invariance decreases both the probability and the magnitude of participants' judgment changes. Additionally, we hypothesized that the influence would be weakened with increasing expertise of participants. In three preregistered experiments, (G)LMM analyses suggested that increasing judgment invariance decreased the probability and magnitude of judgment changes confirming our hypothesized main effects. Concerning the interaction hypothesis of judgment invariance and expertise, a more ambiguous picture emerged. Experiment 1 was completely consistent with the interaction hypothesis. Experiment 2 supported it concerning the probability but not the magnitude of participants' judgment changes. In Experiment 3, a directionally reversed interaction effect was observed, possibly due to unconscientious participation. We conclude that the insight into the past development of a sequential chain, specifically information on judgment invariance, influences the judgment behavior of contributors in sequential collaborations. In summary, judgment invariance could be established as a substantial influence in sequential collaboration, which comes with practical implications for real‐world collaborative projects.
https://openalex.org/W7213759166 2024 2024-01-01 https://doi.org/10.3917/anpsy1.244.0591 Cincuenta años de trabajo sobre el sesgo de anclaje: ¿Qué hay de nuevo desde Tversky y Kahneman (1974)? | authors: Aglaé Navarre, André Didierjean, Cyril Thomas
  abstract: En 1974, Tversky y Kahneman publicaron un artículo que iba a tener una influencia duradera en el campo de la toma de decisiones. Estos autores destacaron el hecho de que el razonamiento humano se basa muy a menudo en el uso de heurísticos, atajos mentales eficaces, con su contrapartida negativa: la existencia de numerosos sesgos cognitivos. Entre los sesgos cognitivos que intervienen en la toma de decisiones en condiciones de incertidumbre, el más famoso es sin duda el sesgo de anclaje. La solidez y ubicuidad de este efecto lo convierten en un fenómeno especialmente fascinante, que ha dado lugar a una abundante bibliografía desde esta investigación inicial. ¿En qué punto nos encontramos en la celebración del aniversario cincuenta del descubrimiento del sesgo de anclaje? Este artículo revisa la literatura sobre este sesgo. Describimos las principales características de este fenómeno, las diversas teorías que lo explican y proponemos algunas vías para futuras investigaciones.

 Article de revue
Cinquante ans de travaux sur l’effet d’ancrage. Quoi de neuf depuis Tversky et Kahneman (1974) ?
Par Aglaé Navarre, André Didierjean et Cyril Thomas

Pages 591 à 634

Article
Résumé
Auteur(e)s
Sur un sujet proche

Ajouter au panier

Au quotidien, nous sommes très fréquemment amenés à prendre des décisions. Certaines de ces décisions ont peu d’impact (e.g., un ou deux sucres dans notre café ?), d’autres beaucoup plus (e.g., faut-il surenchérir pour un achat immobilier qui engage un emprunt sur 25 ans ?). Certaines ont des répercussions plus importantes encore, en ce qu’elles mettent en jeu le futur d’autres personnes. C’est le cas par exemple des décisions prises dans le domaine médical ou dans le domaine judiciaire. Pour prendre ces décisions, nous sommes confrontés à une difficulté importante, nous disposons d’une « rationalité limitée », pour reprendre les termes d’Herbert Simon (1955), premier psychologue à recevoir un prix Nobel d’économie. Le nombre d’informations qu’il est possible de maintenir dans son esprit en même temps est très réduit, rendant compliqué de manipuler mentalement tous les paramètres en jeu. Pourtant, nous interagissons de façon tout à fait satisfaisante avec notre environnement au quotidien ; nous savons être créatif, imaginatif, actif et résolvons très vite la plupart des difficultés que nous rencontrons. L’une des explications avancées à ce paradoxe est la coexistence de deux modes de pensée bien distincts, communément appelés système 1 et système 2 (e.g., Evans, 2008 ; Kahneman, 2011 ; Stanovich, 1999).
Le système 1 correspond à un système de pensée intuitif et automatique qui permet de prendre des décisions rapides grâce à l’utilisation de raccourcis mentaux appelés heuristiques…

Research Reports
Testing the Reliability of Anchoring Susceptibility Scores
Lucia Weber 1,2, Lukas Röseler 1,2
[1] Department of Personality Psychology and Psychological Assessment, University of Bamberg, Bamberg, Germany. [2] Münster Center for Open Science,
University of Münster, Münster, Germany.
Europe's Journal of Psychology, 2025, Vol. 21(1), 1–10, https://doi.org/10.5964/ejop.9891
Received: 2022-07-11 • Accepted: 2024-11-14 • Published (VoR): 2025-02-28
Handling Editor: Johannes Karl, Dublin City University, Dublin, Ireland
Corresponding Author: Lucia Weber, Gutenbergstrasse 26, 3011 Bern, Switzerland. Tel. +41(0)783359128. E-mail: [email redacted]
Supplementary Materials: Code, Data, Materials, Preregistration [see Index of Supplementary Materials]
Abstract
Whereas anchoring is a very robust and well-known effect that refers to the assimilation of numeric estimates toward previously
considered numbers, the psychological mechanisms behind it have yet to be fully clarified. Research on theories on how susceptibility
to anchoring is related to other personality parameters has not been able to provide sufficient empirical evidence of such
relationships. A probable explanation is that anchoring scores lack reliability in most anchoring experiments. The present research
examined whether reliability depends on the type of score used to capture anchoring susceptibility. In a classical anchoring
experiment, men and women aged between 14 and 67 years (N = 78) were asked to estimate the true values of certain numbers (e.g.,
height of the Zugspitze mountain) after being confronted with either a high or a low anchor number. Four different anchoring scores
that are commonly used to measure susceptibility to anchoring in anchoring research were computed for every person, as well as the
scores’ reliabilities. The number and types of items were chosen to allow for reliable and valid measurement. Anchoring effects were
present, but the reliabilities of all four scores were either very low or zero. These results reinforce the reliability problem that was also
described by previous research. So far, there are no conditions under which anchoring susceptibility can be measured reliably,
suggesting the development of new measures or even questioning the existence of individual differences in susceptibility to
anchoring. In further research, other person-independent factors that may influence anchoring strength should be investigated to
develop theories that can explain the psychological mechanisms behind anchoring.
Keywords
anchoring, anchoring effect, anchoring scores, anchoring strength, reliability
Anchoring describes the phenomenon that people are influenced by a previously considered number when making a
numerical estimate. In studies on the anchoring effect, people are initially confronted with an anchor number—often
by having to respond to a comparative question, such as “Is the height of Mount Everest larger or smaller than 5,000
meters?” After answering this first question, when asked to give an actual estimate, people tend to assimilate their
answer toward the anchor.
It has been proposed that people differ in the extent to which they are susceptible to this effect, depending on certain
individual differences, such as general knowledge, cognitive abilities (e.g., Bergman et al., 2010), or the Big Five (e.g.,
McElroy & Dowd, 2007). The implicit assumption that susceptibility to anchoring is a person parameter can be found
at the core of anchoring models, which aim to clarify which psychological mechanisms underlie anchoring effects, for
example, in the Insufficient Adjustment Model (Epley & Gilovich, 2001).

content.content:
NUMERICAL ASSIMILATION
2
Abstract
People’s quantitative estimates, such as judgments about the height of a tower or the
distance between two cities, can be influenced by external values, including random numbers in
the environment or another person’s estimate. We reviewed three distinct but related phenomena
in quantitative estimation: anchoring effects, advice taking, and hindsight bias. These effects are
assimilative, meaning estimates are drawn toward the external value. They are also robust and
they exhibit medium to large effect sizes. However, previous studies suggest that the reliability
of their measurements differs considerably, ranging from low (anchoring) to high (advice
taking). In this project, we compared the reliabilities of the three phenomena using open data
(Study 1) and a new experiment employing a homogenized paradigm (Study 2). Homogenization
involves controlling for differences in the informativeness of external values, computing
assimilation scores, and using the same setting and knowledge domain. In Study 1, we found that
anchoring effects were largely unreliable, advice taking was reliably measured, and hindsight
bias showed moderate reliability, consistent with prior research. This overall pattern was
[reproduced] in [the simulation of] Study 2. We conclude that although methodological factors
contribute to variability, they alone cannot explain differences in reliability.
Keywords: reliability, numerical assimilation, anchoring effect, advice taking, hindsight
bias, judgment and decision-making

https://openalex.org/W4400496102 2024 2024-07-10 https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/69jwr Navigating Anchor Relevance Skillfully: Expertise Reduces Susceptibility to Anchoring Effects | authors: Maren Mayer, Tobias R. Rebholz
  abstract: 50 years ago Tversky and Kahneman (1974) described anchoring as the phenomenon whereby an irrelevant numerical value influences a subsequent numerical judgment. Although expertise strongly influences the accuracy of judgments, its role in anchoring is still unclear with findings of reduced, similar, and stronger anchoring in experts compared to novices. Moreover, three prominent theories of anchoring, i.e., the Insufficient Adjustment Model, the Selective Accessibility Model, and the Scale Distortion Theory, make different predictions regarding the influence of expertise on anchoring. To address this inconsistency and to test these theories of anchoring against each other, we manipulate individuals' expertise prior to a perceptual estimation task. Additionally, we manipulate anchor relevance and anchor extremity. In two preregistered experiments, we find that experts do indeed show less anchoring compared to novices, and that more extreme anchors lead to stronger anchoring effects. However, we do not find an effect of anchor relevance in either experiment. These results add to the growing body of literature showing that expertise reduces anchoring effects. Morevoer, although no anchoring theory is clearly supported in the experiments, the results are mostly consistent with the Insufficient Adjustment Model assuming ranges of plausible values and the Scale Distortion Theory. Our findings highlight the importance of expertise in judgments in general and anchoring in particular. Thus, theories of anchoring should take expertise into account as a strong inhibitor of anchoring effects.

content.content:
conceptual and paradigmatic similarities.
Harvey and Fischer’s (1997) advice taking index dominated the recent literature
(e.g., Hütter & Ache, 2016; Schultze et al., 2015; Soll & Larrick, 2009; see Bailey et al.,
2022, for a review). Their index, as formally introduced below, reflects how strongly people
adapted their judgment (i.e., the endogenous component) in units of the distance between
the exogenous components, that is, the advice they received and their independent initial
judgment. We suspect that it is the simplicity of this ratio-of-differences (ROD) formula
paired with its capability to capture inter- and intra-individual differences1 that is
responsible for its popularity. The same reasoning applies to other popular criteria from
traditional ROD-type modeling such as the “anchoring index” of Jacowitz and Kahneman
(1995) or the “hindsight bias index” of Hell et al. (1988). However, intermixing endogenous
and exogenous components for building ROD scores implies a number of conceptual and
measurement problems (Cronbach, 1943; Cronbach & Furby, 1970; Edwards, 1995;
Firebaugh & Gibbs, 1985). For instance, ratios are often not normally distributed (see Soll
& Larrick, 2009, for the characteristic W-shaped distribution of ROD-WOA) and imply a
linear relationship between numerator and denominator (but see Schultze et al., 2015, for
test moderation effects on the WOA or to compare different weighting policies.
Often people combine different sources of information in a nonlinear way (e.g.,
Ganzach, 1995, for clinical judgment). Actually, ROD-WOA usually features an
inverse-U-shaped relation with advice distance in many empirical studies: Close as well as
more distant advice is typically taken less than advice of “intermediate” distance (Hütter &
Ache, 2016; Moussaïd et al., 2013; Rebholz, 2023; Schultze et al., 2015). As the regression
framework allows to incorporate any number and type of additional predictors on any level,
researchers no longer have to assume response linear processing of advice for calculating
the weights. To model nonlinear weighting as requested by Bailey et al. (2022), the set of
additional predictors can include higher-order terms such as polynomials (e.g., Schreiner
et al., 2023) or nonlinear transformations of advice (distance). Base expansions provide an
even more flexible solution in the “generalized additive modeling” framework (e.g., Baayen
& Linke, 2020). In essence, as already requested by Slovic and Lichtenstein (1971), the
proposed multilevel modeling approach allows statistical tests of alternative theoretical
accounts of external information utilization.

SUSCEPTILITY TO ANCHORING EFFECTS
Testing the Reliability of Anchoring Susceptibility Scores
Lucia Weber1 and Lukas Röseler2
1
Faculty of Medicine, University of Zurich, Switzerland
2
Münster Center for Open Science, University of Münster, Germany
Author Note
Lucia Weber
Lukas Röseler
https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6446-1901
Correspondence concerning this article should be addressed to Lukas Röseler, University
of Münster. Email: [email redacted]
Preprint Version
This manuscript corresponds to the corrected version of the article published in EJOP
(February 2025). This manuscript has not been peer reviewed in this form.
 SUSCEPTIBILITY TO ANCHORING EFFECTS
Abstract
Whereas anchoring is a very robust and well-known effect that refers to the assimilation of
numeric estimates toward previously considered numbers, the psychological mechanisms
behind it have yet to be fully clarified. Research on theories on how susceptibility to
anchoring is related to other personality parameters has not been able to provide sufficient
empirical evidence of such relationships. A probable explanation is that anchoring scores lack
reliability in most anchoring experiments. The present research examined whether reliability
depends on the type of score used to capture anchoring susceptibility. In a classical anchoring
experiment, men and women aged between 14 and 67 years (N = 78) were asked to estimate
the true values of certain numbers (e.g., height of the Zugspitze mountain) after being
confronted with either a high or a low anchor number. Four different anchoring scores that are
commonly used to measure susceptibility to anchoring in anchoring research were computed
for every person, as well as the scores’ reliabilities. The number and types of items were
chosen to allow for reliable and valid measurement. Anchoring effects were present, but the
reliabilities of all four scores were either very low or zero. These results reinforce the
reliability problem that was also described by previous research. So far, there are no
conditions under which anchoring susceptibility can be measured reliably, suggesting the
development of new measures or even questioning the existence of individual differences in
susceptibility to anchoring. In further research, other person-independent factors that may
influence anchoring strength should be investigated to develop theories that can explain the
psychological mechanisms behind anchoring.
Keywords: anchoring, anchoring effect, anchoring scores, anchoring strength, reliability

content.text:
I found 24 works that cite OpAQ or the meta-analysis preprint. None reuses OpAQ's human estimates to relate the proportional anchoring index to anchor extremity at the item level. The only paper that reanalyses OpAQ's human estimates is the Röseler et al. 2024 Meta-Psychology reliability paper. Two LLM papers take only the OpAQ question/anchor/true-value items. The closest prior work comes from citers who used their own data: Barrera-Lemarchand et al. 2024 and Navarre et al. 2024.

**Coverage.** I combined OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar (OpAQ DOI only), Google Scholar "cited by" via SerpAPI, and web searches.
- Semantic Scholar does not find the meta-analysis by its DOI, and its title search hit rate limits. Google Scholar stood in: all 14 + 3 citers in the meta-analysis's two clusters were retrieved.
- As of today, OpenAlex, Crossref and Google Scholar show no published version of the meta-analysis (10.31234/osf.io/wf2tn).
- Page numbers are PDF pages unless stated otherwise.
- The Correction lists data contributors as co-authors. These include Barrera-Lemarchand, Onuki, Ueda, Speekenbrink and Harris, so citations by those authors come from dataset contributors, not independent reusers.

## A. Works citing OpAQ (10.5334/jopd.67) and/or the meta-analysis (wf2tn)

| # | Work (source) | Class | Summary / key numbers |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Röseler et al. 2024, Correction to OpAQ, JOPD, [10.5334/jopd.92](https://doi.org/10.5334/jopd.92) (OA, S2, GS) | n/a | Corrects the author list only. Ten co-authors had been left out "due to an administrative error" (Ambrus, McKay, Hartig, Allen, Rostekova, Pearton, Ponader, Imhoff, Seida, Speekenbrink) (p. 2). No item counts, trial counts or variables changed. |
| 2 | Röseler, Weber, Helgerth, Stich et al. 2024, *Measurements of Susceptibility to Anchoring are Unreliable*, Meta-Psychology 8, [10.15626/MP.2022.3236](https://doi.org/10.15626/MP.2022.3236) (OA, GS) | **REUSED-OPAQ (human estimates)** | Reliability meta-analysis of person-level scores: 41 studies, N = 9,825, median 6 items (p. 5). Four scores: adjustment, absolute adjustment, a "0-1 score" = (estimate − anchor)/(true − anchor), and a restricted 0-1 score (p. 4). Mean interitem r = .126 overall (REML .137 [.078, .197]). By score: 0-1 = .131, restricted = .164, adjustment = .154 (pp. 5–6). The 0-1 score is proportional but per person, and it is never related to anchor distance. The only extremity remark is in the discussion: "non-linear models that account for the nonlinear influence of extreme anchors … are likely more precise" (p. 11). |
| 3 | Röseler, Incerti, Rebholz, Seida, Papenmeier, *Falsifying the Insufficient Adjustment Model*. Published as Meta-Psychology 9 (2025), [10.15626/MP.2024.4137](https://doi.org/10.15626/MP.2024.4137) (Crossref-verified; preprint jztk2 v1–v3) | CITED-ONLY (it **contributes** data) | Formalises insufficient adjustment as a TOTE unit (test-operate-test-exit loop) with discrete jumps: adjustment = ⌊t/pause⌋·strength until number × pause (p. 3). Four preregistered studies (N = 898) found no time-pressure effect. Mini meta-analysis: r_time = 0.02 [−.045, .086]; r_anchoring = 0.191 [−.211, .594], Q(8) = 177.61 (p. 22). Proposes dropping the assumption of unidirectional adjustment (p. 22). Data from Studies 1, 2 and 4 are in OpAQ (p. 24). Nothing on distance or proportional adjustment. |
| 4 | Mayer & Heck 2025, PBR 32:1142–1164, [10.3758/s13423-024-02619-9](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-024-02619-9) (OA, GS) | CITED-ONLY (meta-analysis) | Computational model of sequential collaboration. Its anchoring term is additive and proportional: A_ik = E_i·(y_{i−1,k} − T_k), so the shift is a fixed, expertise-scaled fraction of the anchor–truth gap, which implies an AI that stays constant with distance (p. 1147, Eq. 9). Cites wf2tn only as a general anchoring reference. No OpAQ data. |
| 5 | Fischer, Mayer, Kimmerle 2026, JBDM, [10.1002/bdm.70063](https://doi.org/10.1002/bdm.70063) (OA, GS) | CITED-ONLY (meta-analysis) | Three preregistered experiments: information on "judgment invariance" lowers the probability and size of changes in sequential collaboration (abstract). Cites wf2tn for "informative anchors induce a higher anchoring effect" (full text read via browser). |
| 6 | Onuki & Ueda 2025, Commun Psychol 3:97, [10.1038/s44271-025-00276-9](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44271-025-00276-9) (OA, S2, GS) | CITED-ONLY | Range-framed limits ("0–60 km/h") versus upper limits, tested on driving speed and handwashing. OpAQ and the Correction are cited only for "this effect is remarkably robust" (p. 1). The meta-analysis's g = 0.59 ("speed") and g = 0.94 ("duration") set the power analyses (pp. 2–5). |
| 7 | Barrera-Lemarchand, Balenzuela, Bahrami, Deroy, Navajas 2024, Psych Sci, [10.1177/09567976241252138](https://doi.org/10.1177/09567976241252138) (OA, S2, GS; preprint [10.31234/osf.io/wvfm3](https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/wvfm3)) | CITED-ONLY, own data. **Most relevant prior work.** | Model: anchored mean = weighted average of anchor and crowd mean, with weight **w = w₀·e^(−β\|A−θ\|)**, "the anchoring extremeness effect (Röseler et al., 2022)" (MS p. 8, Eq. 4). Exp 2: N = 396, 30 percentage questions, anchors fixed at 5% and 95%. The anchoring weight correlates with \|A − θ\| at **r = −0.56, p = 3×10⁻⁶** (MS pp. 15–16). The exponential form beats linear (ΔAIC = 1.9) and hyperbolic (ΔAIC = 0.59), which is weak discrimination. One symmetric weight per question beats separate low/high weights (ΔAIC 1.6, ΔBIC 5.7) (MS p. 16). Caveats below. |
| 8 | Reimer, Oh, Loaiza-Ramírez, Barber 2024, Sustainability, [10.3390/su16062540](https://doi.org/10.3390/su16062540) (OA, GS) | CITED-ONLY (meta-analysis) | N = 384 chose thermostat setpoints. The displayed current temperature and the scale's midpoint and range affected choices; the scale increment did not (abstract). wf2tn is cited for anchors altering numerical estimates and for "various processes". |
| 9 | Navarre, Didierjean, Thomas 2024, L'Année psychologique 124:591–634, [10.3917/anpsy1.244.0591](https://doi.org/10.3917/anpsy1.244.0591) (OA, GS) | CITED-ONLY (review) | Narrative review in French. It cites the reliability paper (#2) together with Chapman & Johnson 1994 and Thorsteinson 2011 for this claim: the anchor-size / effect-size relation is **not linear**; beyond the plausible range the effect grows more slowly, **only for high anchors**, while low anchors stay linear (p. 597; repeated p. 602). It also says implausible anchors give weaker effects (p. 598). No new analysis. The attribution to #2 goes beyond what #2 shows. |
| 10 | Young, Speekenbrink et al. 2026, Cogn Psychol 164:101796, [10.1016/j.cogpsych.2026.101796](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2026.101796) (OA, GS) | CITED-ONLY | Cites wf2tn as a meta-analysis (pp. 1, 18). Uses its own studies plus an own meta-analysis of anchoring-by-items studies. No OpAQ data. |
| 11 | Stöcker 2024, dissertation, [10.20378/irb-96573](https://doi.org/10.20378/irb-96573) (OA) | CITED-ONLY | Advice-taking thesis. wf2tn is cited for "a specific number can function as an anchor" (p. 23). |
| 12 | Shiddieqi, Prastowo, Riyanto 2024, Scientax, [10.52869/st.v5i2.667](https://doi.org/10.52869/st.v5i2.667) (OA) | CITED-ONLY | Tax-compliance paper. wf2tn is in the reference list (ref. 19, p. 10). |
| 13 | Owusu, Wiegreffe, Feldman 2026, *Localizing Anchoring Pathways in Language Models*, arXiv [2606.12818](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.12818) (S2) | **REUSED-OPAQ (items only)** | Turns 100 OpAQ numerical questions into a 9-option multiple-choice format (truth, low and high anchor, intermediate values) and traces anchoring circuits in LLMs (pp. 1, 3). No human estimates, no extremity or proportional analysis. |
| 14 | Owusu & Feldman 2026, ACL short, [10.18653/v1/2026.acl-short.16](https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2026.acl-short.16) (S2) | **REUSED-OPAQ (items only)** | 50 randomly sampled OpAQ items, replicated on 99 items (1,188 observations). Anchoring is measured as a shift in the model's output distribution (total variation distance, TVD) and in expected value. Susceptibility falls with model confidence (β ≈ −0.05, p < .001), and high anchors dominate (pp. 2–3). No distance analysis. |
| 15 | Vaccaro 2026, *Preregistration for Experiments with AI Agents*, SSRN [10.2139/ssrn.6732238](https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6732238) (S2) | CITED-ONLY | Specification curve over 2,430 LLM anchoring configurations, with anchor distance (high/medium/low) as one factor across 5 questions. Anchoring indices run from negative to >1.0. OpAQ is cited for a "human range 0.3–0.6" (pp. 13–14). No effect of distance is reported separately. |
| 16 | Rebholz, Groß, Röseler, *Assimilation to External Cues*, Stage 1 registered report, PsyArXiv 5u8br (v2 2025 read; v3 [10.31234/osf.io/5u8br_v3](https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/5u8br_v3), Feb 2026) (GS) | CITED-ONLY (OpAQ summary used for power) | Study 1 anchoring data are Weber & Röseler 2025 (N = 78), not the pooled OpAQ file (p. 20). The OpAQ Shiny meta-analytic d = 0.60 [0.58, 0.78] feeds the power analysis (p. 28). Says "extremely high or low anchors tend to lead to smaller effects" (Chapman & Johnson; wf2tn; Mayer & Rebholz 2024) (p. 6). |
| 17 | Rebholz, Biella, Hütter, mixed-effects regression weights, JBDM 2024, [10.1002/bdm.2369](https://doi.org/10.1002/bdm.2369) (GS only) | Probably a Google Scholar mis-link | OpAQ appears neither in the preprint text (x36az) nor in the JBDM Crossref reference list. Methodologically relevant: it argues that ratio indices such as the Jacowitz–Kahneman anchoring index assume linearity, and proposes mixed-effects regression weights that can include nonlinear distance terms (preprint lines ~105–120, ~1835–1850). |
| 18 | Röseler 2023, z-curve validation, MetaArXiv [10.31222/osf.io/ewb2t](https://doi.org/10.31222/osf.io/ewb2t) (GS) | CITED-ONLY, not read | Topic is replication-rate prediction. |
| 19 | Haidinger et al. 2026, EJOR, [10.1016/j.ejor.2026.06.002](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejor.2026.06.002) (GS) | CITED-ONLY, not read | Cognitive effort in multi-criteria decisions. |
| 20 | Edmar, Enquist, Luke 2025, misinformation-effect meta-analysis, PsyArXiv m68kf (GS) | CITED-ONLY, not read | Different topic. |
| 21 | Röseler et al. 2024, Epley & Gilovich replication, JCRE, [10.18718/81781.38](https://doi.org/10.18718/81781.38) (GS; DataCite-verified) | CITED-ONLY | Replication of moderators (need for cognition, cognitive load, forewarning). |
| 22 | Weber & Röseler 2025, EJOP 21(1), [10.5964/ejop.9891](https://doi.org/10.5964/ejop.9891) (web) | Contributes data; OpAQ used for power only | New study, N = 78, 18 items, reliability of the four scores. The power analysis uses score correlations from OpAQ as of 27 Aug 2021 (p. 2). |

Two more hits turned out not to cite OpAQ: Lou et al. arXiv 2412.06593 and "Anchors in the Machine" arXiv 2511.05766. Schley & Weingarten 2026 (Management Science, [10.1287/mnsc.2023.03238](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.03238)) cites neither work according to its 90 Crossref references.

**Barrera-Lemarchand caveats (#7):**
- The numbers come from the accepted Word manuscript (49 pp., April 2024), not the typeset Psych Sci version. Page numbers are manuscript pages, and I could not check the published version.
- Their "anchoring weight" is one-sided: w_j = (μ_j − μ)/(A_j − μ), measured against the unanchored mean (MS p. 43, Eq. 16). It is not the two-anchor AI.
- Distance varies only through the true value θ, because the anchors stay at 5 and 95 on a 0–100 scale.

**Relevant study that does not cite OpAQ:** Mayer & Rebholz 2024, PsyArXiv [10.31234/osf.io/69jwr](https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/69jwr), unpublished as far as I can find. Two preregistered perceptual-estimation experiments manipulated anchor extremity and found "more extreme anchors lead to stronger anchoring effects" (abstract only). It is unclear whether this is absolute or proportional.

## B. Röseler anchoring works 2022–2026

- **OpAQ data paper** (2022): JOPD, [10.5334/jopd.67](https://doi.org/10.5334/jopd.67). Correction 2024, [10.5334/jopd.92](https://doi.org/10.5334/jopd.92).
- **Hanging the Anchor Off a New Ship** (Röseler & Schütz): preprint only, [10.31234/osf.io/wf2tn](https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/wf2tn). OSF file qswer is `OpAQ_metaanalysis_v1.pdf`, attached to preprint wf2tn_v1.
- **Measurements of Susceptibility to Anchoring are Unreliable**: preprint b6t35 (2022), published Meta-Psychology 2024, [10.15626/MP.2022.3236](https://doi.org/10.15626/MP.2022.3236).
- **Testing the Reliability of Anchoring Susceptibility Scores** (Weber & Röseler): preprint 2kfh3 (2022), published EJOP 2025, [10.5964/ejop.9891](https://doi.org/10.5964/ejop.9891). There is also an **unpublished corrected version** (`Preprint_Corrigendum.pdf`, Jan 2026) in OpAQ component sz5b9, next to corrected script and data files dated Aug–Dec 2025.
  - The corrected Table 1 assigns different effect sizes to items. Examples: Danube −0.32 → 1.12; Russia–US distance 1.24 → −0.32; lottery 0.89 → −0.26 (published p. 4 vs corrigendum p. 10). Its text does not say what went wrong.
  - This matters for an item-level OpAQ analysis. Without opening data I cannot tell whether the OpAQ master file (ygnvb, last modified 2023-11-22) has the corrected item mapping.
- **Falsifying the Insufficient Adjustment Model**: preprint jztk2 (2023, v2/v3 2025), published Meta-Psychology 9 (2025), [10.15626/MP.2024.4137](https://doi.org/10.15626/MP.2024.4137).
- **Replicating Epley & Gilovich**: preprint bgp3m (2022), published JCRE 2024, [10.18718/81781.38](https://doi.org/10.18718/81781.38).
- **Assimilation and Contrast are Everywhere** (Röseler & Schütz): preprint 2024, [10.31234/osf.io/krwcn](https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/krwcn). Theory review. It mentions distance only via Sherif et al. 1958 on assimilation vs contrast depending on anchor distance (p. 5) and "implausible and extreme anchors … weaker anchoring effects" (Chapman & Johnson) (pp. 10, 13). No OpAQ analysis.
- **Assimilation to External Cues** (Rebholz, Groß, Röseler): Stage 1 registered report, v3 Feb 2026 (#16 above).
- **PREreview of "Anchoring-Based Causal Design (ABCD)"** (2026): Zenodo [10.5281/zenodo.21281801](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21281801). A review of someone else's preprint; not read.
- **"Absolute versus Relative Adjustment from Anchors"** (Röseler & Wagner, OSF project [dsyrk](https://osf.io/dsyrk)): an OSF project, not a 2026 preprint. OpenAlex dates it 2026-08-12, which is only the last-modified date; the project was created in Oct 2020.
  - The wiki says: "Contains data and analyses that explored the relationship between anchor distance and anchor effect strength."
  - File names show two pretests (Nov–Dec 2020), a main study (analysis scripts Jan 2021), `simulation_absrel_v5.R` (Dec 2020), and a reanalysis script for Teovanović 2015 data. I did not open any of these files.
  - There is no manuscript and I found no write-up anywhere (web, OpenAlex, Röseler's publication page). This is the closest unpublished precursor to the planned study.
- **"Anchoring Effects Meta Analysis"** (OSF project [63um5](https://osf.io/63um5)): also modified on 2026-08-12. The wiki says the meta-analysis was withdrawn and replaced by "a mega-analysis of openly available datasets" (that is, wf2tn). Only the 2021 preregistration materials are there.

## C. OpAQ OSF project (ygnvb; metadata and wiki only)

- The wiki lists "effects of anchor extremeness" among the hypotheses the dataset can be used to test. It does not list any publications.
- Components: sz5b9 "OpAQ Study" (the EJOP study and its corrigendum), 4t5mu "OpAQ Meta-Analysis", gnr2x "OpAQ Reliability Analysis".
- Linked preprints: b6t35 (reliability paper) and 2kfh3 (EJOP study).

**Novelty conclusion:**
- No work tests the two-anchor proportional AI against anchor extremity on OpAQ's human item-level estimates, and none compares process models on it.
- Prior evidence on extremity:
  - Barrera-Lemarchand 2024: one-sided weight falls with distance, r = −.56, on a bounded percentage scale.
  - Mayer & Rebholz 2024: extreme anchors give stronger effects (abstract only; absolute or proportional unclear).
  - Navarre 2024: review claim of saturation for high anchors only.
  - The meta-analysis: study-level Hedges' g against mean relative distance.
- The unpublished dsyrk project shows the OpAQ team explored anchor distance against effect strength in 2020–21.

I did not open any data file. The files I read are the PDFs of the corrigendum and of the 2023 Rebholz preprint, plus OSF metadata and wiki text. Scratch files are in /tmp/jdmsim/scratch_nov_cit_*; the draft summary is /tmp/jdmsim/scratch_nov_cit_findings.md.

Sources: [OpAQ JOPD](https://openpsychologydata.metajnl.com/articles/10.5334/jopd.67), [Correction PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12270249/), [Meta-Psychology IAM](https://open.lnu.se/index.php/metapsychology/article/view/4137/4300), [Röseler research page](https://lukasroeseler.github.io/home/research.html), [Owusu et al. arXiv](https://arxiv.org/html/2606.12818), [EJOP 2025](https://ejop.psychopen.eu/index.php/ejop/article/download/9891/9891.pdf), [Mayer & Rebholz on Sciety](https://sciety.org/articles/activity/10.31234/osf.io/69jwr), [Navarre Cairn](https://shs.cairn.info/revue-l-annee-psychologique-2024-4-page-591?lang=fr), [OSF ygnvb](https://osf.io/ygnvb/)

content.text:
I found 24 works that cite OpAQ or the meta-analysis. None relates the two-anchor proportional anchoring index (AI) to anchor extremity on OpAQ's human item-level estimates, and none fits process models to them. Only one citer reuses OpAQ's human estimates: the 2024 reliability paper (row 2 below). Two LLM papers reuse OpAQ items only.

**How I searched.** I used OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar (the OpAQ DOI only), Google Scholar "cited by" via SerpAPI, and web searches. Semantic Scholar does not find the meta-analysis by its DOI (10.31234/osf.io/wf2tn), so I used Google Scholar's two clusters for it (14 + 3 citers, all retrieved). The meta-analysis has not been published: I found no journal version in OpenAlex, Crossref or Google Scholar. I opened no data files; reading covered papers, OSF node metadata, wiki text and file names. Page numbers are PDF pages.

## Priority 1: Barrera-Lemarchand et al. 2024, Psych Sci
DOI [10.1177/09567976241252138](https://doi.org/10.1177/09567976241252138). **Classification: CITED-ONLY, own data.**

I read the accepted Word manuscript (49 pp., April 2024; preprint [10.31234/osf.io/wvfm3](https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/wvfm3)). The typeset version was blocked, so page numbers are manuscript pages and I could not check the published wording.

- **OpAQ items or data: not used.**
  - OpAQ is cited only as a reference (MS p. 31). "Röseler et al., 2022" is cited in the text as the source of the "anchoring extremeness effect" (pp. 6, 8, 15).
  - Exp 2 items are 30 Argentina-specific survey percentages (SI Table S4).
  - Barrera-Lemarchand, Navajas and Freira are OpAQ co-authors under the 2024 Correction, so their data are probably in OpAQ.
- **Model (MS p. 8, Eq. 4):** the anchored mean is w·A + (1−w)·μ, where μ is the unanchored crowd mean and w = w₀·e^(−β|A_j − θ|).
  - θ is the true value. β is described as sensitivity to anchor–truth distance, "the anchoring extremeness effect".
  - Simulation values: θ = 324, μ = 250, A_L = 10, A_H = 1000, w₀ = 1, β = 0.0017.
- **Exp 2 design (MS pp. 13–14):**
  - N = 396 recruited online in Argentina (119 in Group 1, 277 in Group 2).
  - 30 general-knowledge percentage questions, split into two sets of 15, bounded 0–100.
  - The anchors were the same for every question: 5% (low) and 95% (high). Low or high was assigned at random per question. The control group gave estimates without anchors.
  - Preregistered: aspredicted RYC_4Y5.
- **Distance:** raw |A_j − θ| in percentage points, not normalised.
  - Because the anchors are fixed, distance varies only through the true value θ. Anchor position was never manipulated.
  - The Fig. 3D caption (MS p. 17) plots each question's weight (low-anchor dots, high-anchor dots) against distance, with a log scale on the weight axis and a linear fit.
- **Anchoring weight:** one-sided, per anchor and per question: w_j = (μ_j − μ)/(A_j − μ), measured against the unanchored mean μ (SI p. 43, Eq. 16).
  - The authors call it "very similar" to the Jacowitz–Kahneman anchoring index (MS p. 15).
  - It is 0 when the anchor has no effect and 1 when the mean equals the anchor.
  - It is **not** the two-anchor AI (high − low)/(A_H − A_L).
- **Main result:** the weight correlates with distance at **r = −0.56, p = 3×10⁻⁶** (MS p. 16).
  - The text gives no n; about 60 points (30 questions × 2 anchors) is my inference, not stated.
  - Supporting pattern: for true values below 50% (17 questions), the low-anchor group's estimates did not differ from the truth (t(16) = 0.95, p = .36, BF₀₁ = 2.7). The mirror pattern held for the 13 questions above 50% (MS pp. 14–15).
- **Model comparison (MS p. 16):** the exponential form fits best, but the margins are small.
  - Against linear: ΔAIC = ΔBIC = 1.9.
  - Against hyperbolic w₀/(1 + β|A − θ|) (their Eq. 7): ΔAIC = ΔBIC = 0.59.
  - One weight per question beats separate low and high weights (ΔAIC = 1.6, ΔBIC = 5.7).

## Priority 2: Mayer & Rebholz 2024 (does not cite OpAQ)
PsyArXiv [10.31234/osf.io/69jwr](https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/69jwr), full text read. No journal version found.

- **Task and design:** random-dot estimation (100–599 dots, 25 anchoring images) in a 2 (expertise) × 2 (anchor relevance) × 2 (anchor extremity) design (p. 11).
  - Extremity: anchors deviate ±35% ("low") or ±70% ("high") from the true value, coded −0.5/0.5 (p. 14).
  - Preregistered: aspredicted GZQ_48M.
- **Outcome:** absolute relative error = |judgment/correct × 100 − 100|, i.e. percent deviation from the truth (p. 14).
- **Results:**

| Experiment | Extremity effect (percentage points) | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Exp 1 | β = 4.88, 95% CI [2.80, 6.97], t(23.79) = 4.60, p < .001 | p. 15 |
| Exp 2 | β = 7.37, 95% CI [4.53, 10.20], t(24.00) = 5.09, p < .001 | p. 21 |

- **Exploratory slope (Exp 1):** relative error on signed anchor deviation, β = 0.15 [0.09, 0.21], t(23.08) = 5.13 (page not pinned; around p. 17).
- **My reading, not the authors':** doubling the anchor's distance (35% → 70%) raises absolute error by only about 5–7 points. That is a pull of roughly 0.14–0.21 per unit of extra distance, i.e. a roughly constant proportional pull. "Stronger anchoring" here is absolute, not proportional.

# Citers of OpAQ (10.5334/jopd.67) and meta-analysis (10.31234/osf.io/wf2tn): novelty check

Sources: OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar (OpAQ DOI only; S2 does not index wf2tn by DOI, title search rate-limited), Google Scholar cited-by via SerpAPI (OpAQ cluster 5670922102386136969, 7 citers; wf2tn clusters 9079720239863130570 and 5707472742057289217, 14 + 3 citers, all retrieved), web search. No data files opened. Page refs = PDF pages.

## Bottom line
No citer relates the two-anchor proportional AI to anchor extremity on OpAQ human item-level estimates, and none fits process models to them. The only reuse of OpAQ human estimates is Röseler et al. 2024 Meta-Psychology (reliability). Two LLM papers reuse OpAQ items only. wf2tn has no published version (OpenAlex/Crossref/GS). OpAQ OSF wiki (ygnvb) names "effects of anchor extremeness" as a testable hypothesis and lists no publications using the dataset. Closest prior work uses own data: Barrera-Lemarchand 2024 (one-sided weight falls with distance, r = -.56), Mayer & Rebholz 2024 (not an OpAQ citer), and the unpublished Röseler & Wagner OSF project dsyrk (anchor distance vs effect strength, 2020-21, no write-up).

## Priority 1: Barrera-Lemarchand et al. 2024, Psych Sci, 10.1177/09567976241252138 (CITED-ONLY, own data)
Read: author-accepted Word manuscript (49 pp., Apr 2024; preprint 10.31234/osf.io/wvfm3). Page refs are manuscript pages; published typeset version not verified.
- OpAQ items/data: NOT used. OpAQ only in refs (MS p. 31); "Röseler et al., 2022" cited in text for the "anchoring extremeness effect" (pp. 6, 8, 15). Barrera-Lemarchand, Navajas, Freira are OpAQ co-authors (Correction), so their data likely feed OpAQ.
- Model (MS p. 8, Eq. 4): anchored mean mu_j = w_j*A_j + (1-w_j)*mu, with w_j = w0 * exp(-beta*|A_j - theta|); theta = true value, beta = sensitivity to anchor-truth distance ("anchoring extremeness effect"). Simulation: theta=324, mu=250, A_L=10, A_H=1000, w0=1, beta=0.0017.
- Exp 2 design (MS pp. 13-14): N = 396 online, Argentina; 30 percentage questions (0-100), two sets of 15 (Group 1 n=119, Group 2 n=277); fixed anchors 5% (low) and 95% (high) for all questions; low/high assignment random per question; control group unanchored; 20 s per question; preregistered aspredicted RYC_4Y5.
- Distance: raw |A_j - theta| in percentage points, not normalised. Anchors fixed, so distance varies only via theta. Fig. 3D (caption MS p. 17): weight per question (blue = low, red = high anchor) vs distance, log scale on weight, linear fit.
- Anchoring weight (SI p. 43, Eq. 16): w_j = (mu_j - mu)/(A_j - mu), one-sided per anchor and per question, against unanchored mean mu; called "very similar" to Jacowitz-Kahneman index (MS p. 15). 0 = no effect, 1 = mean equals anchor. NOT the two-anchor AI.
- Result (MS p. 16): r = -0.56, p = 3e-6 between weight and |A - theta| (n not stated; ~60 points = 30 questions x 2 anchors is my inference). Supporting (MS pp. 14-15): true value < 50% (17 questions): low-anchor group not different from truth, t(16)=0.95, p=.36, BF01=2.7; > 50% (13 questions): high-anchor group t(12)=2.01, p=.07.
- Model comparison (MS p. 16): exponential best; vs linear dAIC = dBIC = 1.9; vs hyperbolic w0/(1+beta|A-theta|) (their Eq. 7) dAIC = dBIC = 0.59. Weak discrimination. Single symmetric weight per question beats separate low/high weights (dAIC 1.6, dBIC 5.7).

## Priority 2: Mayer & Rebholz 2024, PsyArXiv 10.31234/osf.io/69jwr (does NOT cite OpAQ; full text read; no journal version found)
- Random-dot estimation (100-599 dots; 25 anchoring images) (p. 11). 2 expertise x 2 relevance x 2 extremity; extremity = anchors deviating +/-35% ("low") vs +/-70% ("high") from truth, coded -0.5/0.5 (p. 14). Preregistered aspredicted GZQ_48M.
- DV: absolute relative error = |judgment/correct*100 - 100| (p. 14).
- Exp 1 extremity: beta = 4.88 pp, 95% CI [2.80, 6.97], t(23.79) = 4.60, p < .001 (p. 15). Exp 2: beta = 7.37, [4.53, 10.20], t(24.00) = 5.09, p < .001 (p. 21).
- Exploratory (Exp 1): relative error on signed anchor deviation beta = 0.15 [0.09, 0.21], t(23.08) = 5.13 (page not pinned, ~p. 17).
- My reading, not the authors': doubling anchor distance (35% -> 70%) adds ~5-7 points of error, i.e. ~0.14-0.21 per unit extra distance: roughly constant proportional pull. "Stronger anchoring" is absolute, not proportional.

## All citing works
| # | Work (source) | Class | Summary |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Röseler et al. 2024, Correction, JOPD, 10.5334/jopd.92 (OA, S2, GS) | n/a | Author list only: 10 co-authors omitted "due to an administrative error" (p. 2). No item/trial/variable changes. |
| 2 | Röseler, Weber, Helgerth, Stich et al. 2024, Meta-Psychology 8, 10.15626/MP.2022.3236 (OA, GS) | REUSED-OPAQ (human estimates) | Reliability of person-level scores: 41 studies, N = 9,825, median 6 items (p. 5). Mean interitem r = .126 (REML .137 [.078, .197]); 0-1 score .131, restricted .164, adjustment .154 (pp. 5-6). 0-1 score = (estimate - anchor)/(true - anchor) (p. 4): proportional, per person, never related to distance. Aside: nonlinear models for extreme anchors "likely more precise" (p. 11). |
| 3 | Röseler, Incerti, Rebholz, Seida, Papenmeier, Meta-Psychology 9 (2025), 10.15626/MP.2024.4137 (Crossref-verified; preprint jztk2 v1-v3) | CITED-ONLY (contributes data) | TOTE formalisation, adjustment = floor(t/pause)*strength (p. 3). 4 studies N = 898: r_time = 0.02 [-.045, .086]; r_anchoring = 0.191 [-.211, .594], Q(8) = 177.61 (p. 22). Proposes bidirectional adjustment (p. 22). Studies 1, 2, 4 data in OpAQ (p. 24). |
| 4 | Mayer & Heck 2025, PBR 32:1142-1164, 10.3758/s13423-024-02619-9 (OA, GS) | CITED-ONLY (wf2tn) | Sequential collaboration model; anchoring A = E_i*(y_prev - T): fixed fraction of anchor-truth gap, implies distance-invariant AI (p. 1147, Eq. 9). No OpAQ. |
| 5 | Fischer, Mayer, Kimmerle 2026, JBDM, 10.1002/bdm.70063 (OA, GS) | CITED-ONLY (wf2tn) | Judgment invariance in sequential collaboration; cites wf2tn for "informative anchors induce a higher anchoring effect". |
| 6 | Onuki & Ueda 2025, Commun Psychol 3:97, 10.1038/s44271-025-00276-9 (OA, S2, GS) | CITED-ONLY (OpAQ co-authors) | Range nudges. OpAQ cited for robustness (p. 1); wf2tn g = 0.59 (speed), g = 0.94 (duration) for power (pp. 2-5). |
| 7 | Barrera-Lemarchand et al. 2024 (OA, S2, GS) | CITED-ONLY | See Priority 1. |
| 8 | Reimer et al. 2024, Sustainability, 10.3390/su16062540 (OA, GS) | CITED-ONLY (wf2tn) | N = 384; current temperature, scale midpoint and range affect setpoints; increment does not (abstract). |
| 9 | Navarre, Didierjean, Thomas 2024, Année psychologique 124:591-634, 10.3917/anpsy1.244.0591 (OA, GS) | CITED-ONLY (review) | Claims anchor/effect relation is nonlinear beyond plausible range, high anchors only; low anchors linear (p. 597; p. 602). Cites Chapman & Johnson 1994, Thorsteinson 2011, row 2 (which does not show this). Weaker effects for implausible anchors (p. 598). |
| 10 | Young, Speekenbrink et al. 2026, Cogn Psychol 164:101796, 10.1016/j.cogpsych.2026.101796 (OA, GS) | CITED-ONLY (wf2tn) | Cited pp. 1, 18. Own studies; no OpAQ data. |
| 11 | Stöcker 2024 thesis, 10.20378/irb-96573 (OA) | CITED-ONLY (wf2tn) | Advice taking; p. 23. |
| 12 | Shiddieqi et al. 2024, Scientax, 10.52869/st.v5i2.667 (OA) | CITED-ONLY (wf2tn) | Tax compliance; reference list only. |
| 13 | Owusu, Wiegreffe, Feldman 2026, arXiv 2606.12818 (S2) | REUSED-OPAQ (items only) | 100 OpAQ questions to 9-option multiple choice; LLM circuit localisation (pp. 1, 3). No extremity analysis. |
| 14 | Owusu & Feldman 2026, ACL short, 10.18653/v1/2026.acl-short.16 (S2) | REUSED-OPAQ (items only) | 50 OpAQ items, replicated on 99 (1,188 obs.); anchoring measured as TVD / expected-value shift; falls with model confidence, beta ~ -0.05, p < .001 (pp. 2-3). |
| 15 | Vaccaro 2026, SSRN, 10.2139/ssrn.6732238 (S2) | CITED-ONLY | LLM spec curve, 2,430 configs; anchor distance high/medium/low is one factor; indices from negative to > 1.0; OpAQ cited for "human range 0.3-0.6" (pp. 13-14). |
| 16 | Rebholz, Groß, Röseler, Stage 1 RR, PsyArXiv 5u8br (v2 2025 read; v3 10.31234/osf.io/5u8br_v3, Feb 2026) (GS) | CITED-ONLY (OpAQ summary for power) | Anchoring data = Weber & Röseler 2025 (p. 20); OpAQ Shiny d = 0.60 [0.58, 0.78] for power (p. 28). "extremely high or low anchors tend to lead to smaller effects" (p. 6). |
| 17 | Rebholz, Biella, Hütter, JBDM 2024, 10.1002/bdm.2369 (GS only) | Probable GS mis-link | OpAQ absent from preprint text (x36az) and JBDM Crossref refs. Method point: ratio indices (incl. anchoring index) assume linearity; regression weights allow nonlinear distance terms. |
| 18 | Weber & Röseler 2025, EJOP 21(1), 10.5964/ejop.9891 (web) | Contributes data; OpAQ for power only | N = 78, 18 items; power from OpAQ score correlations (27 Aug 2021) (p. 2). |
| 19 | Röseler 2023 z-curve, MetaArXiv 10.31222/osf.io/ewb2t (GS) | CITED-ONLY, NOT READ | Replication-rate prediction. |
| 20 | Haidinger et al. 2026, EJOR, 10.1016/j.ejor.2026.06.002 (GS) | CITED-ONLY, NOT READ | Multi-criteria decision effort. |
| 21 | Edmar, Enquist, Luke 2025, misinformation meta-analysis, PsyArXiv m68kf (GS) | CITED-ONLY, NOT READ | Different topic. |
| 22 | Röseler et al. 2024, JCRE, 10.18718/81781.38 (GS; DataCite-verified) | CITED-ONLY | Replication of Epley & Gilovich moderators. |

## Röseler anchoring works 2022-2026
- OpAQ: JOPD 2022, 10.5334/jopd.67. Correction 2024, 10.5334/jopd.92.
- Hanging the Anchor Off a New Ship (Röseler & Schütz): preprint only, 10.31234/osf.io/wf2tn. OSF file qswer = OpAQ_metaanalysis_v1.pdf.
- Measurements of Susceptibility to Anchoring are Unreliable: preprint b6t35 (2022); Meta-Psychology 2024, 10.15626/MP.2022.3236.
- Testing the Reliability of Anchoring Susceptibility Scores (Weber & Röseler): preprint 2kfh3 (2022); EJOP 2025, 10.5964/ejop.9891. Unpublished corrected version Preprint_Corrigendum.pdf (Jan 2026, OSF component sz5b9) with corrected script/data (Aug-Dec 2025). Corrected Table 1 reassigns item effect sizes, e.g. Danube -0.32 -> 1.12; Russia-US distance 1.24 -> -0.32; lottery 0.89 -> -0.26 (published p. 4 vs corrected p. 10). Cause not stated. Unknown whether OpAQ master file (ygnvb, last modified 2023-11-22) has the corrected item mapping; relevant for item-level analysis.
- Falsifying the Insufficient Adjustment Model: preprint jztk2 (2023; v2/v3 2025); Meta-Psychology 9 (2025), 10.15626/MP.2024.4137.
- Replicating Epley & Gilovich: preprint bgp3m (2022); JCRE 2024, 10.18718/81781.38.
- Assimilation and Contrast are Everywhere (Röseler & Schütz): preprint 2024, 10.31234/osf.io/krwcn. Theory review; distance only via Sherif et al. 1958 (p. 5) and Chapman & Johnson (pp. 10, 13). No OpAQ analysis.
- Assimilation to External Cues (Rebholz, Groß, Röseler): Stage 1 RR, v3 Feb 2026, 10.31234/osf.io/5u8br_v3.
- PREreview of "Anchoring-Based Causal Design (ABCD)": Zenodo 2026, 10.5281/zenodo.21281801. NOT READ.
- "Absolute versus Relative Adjustment from Anchors" (Röseler & Wagner), OSF project dsyrk: created Oct 2020; OpenAlex 2026 date = last-modified date. Wiki: "data and analyses that explored the relationship between anchor distance and anchor effect strength." File names only (not opened): simulation_absrel_v5.R (Dec 2020), two pretests (Nov-Dec 2020), main study (analysis scripts Jan 2021), reanalysis script for Teovanović 2015. No manuscript; no write-up found anywhere.
- "Anchoring Effects Meta Analysis", OSF project 63um5: wiki says withdrawn; replaced by the mega-analysis (= wf2tn). Only 2021 preregistration materials.

entries.name: SendMessage
entries.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.
